options.text: A birthday attack, prevented by switching to a longer hash function
options.why: A birthday attack looks for hash collisions. Nothing here involves finding collisions.

options.text: A replay attack, prevented by adding fresh nonces to every TLS handshake message
options.why: TLS handshakes already use fresh random values. The problem is the server agreeing to an obsolete protocol.

options.text: A collision attack, prevented by replacing the server certificate
options.why: The certificate is not the weakness. Any certificate would still be used over SSL 3.0 if the server allows it.

takeaway: Downgrade attacks need the server to accept weak protocols. Disabling obsolete versions and cipher suites removes the target.

scenario: A red team enters a secure office using a badge that the system logged as belonging to the CFO, who was at home that day. Earlier, a tester had stood behind the CFO in a coffee shop line with a backpack. The building uses 125 kHz proximity cards.
stem: Which attack MOST likely gave the red team access?

options.text: RFID cloning of the CFO's low-frequency proximity card
options.why: 125 kHz proximity cards transmit a fixed ID with no encryption, so a concealed reader nearby can copy it to a blank card, which the system then logs as the real owner.

options.text: Tailgating behind the CFO through the secure door
options.why: The CFO was at home, and the access log recorded a badge read, so nobody was followed through the door.

options.text: Shoulder surfing the CFO's PIN at the badge reader
options.why: A PIN alone would not produce a badge read in the CFO's name. The card's ID was copied.

options.text: Dumpster diving for an old badge the CFO had thrown away
options.why: Possible in theory, but the backpack in the coffee line is the planted clue, pointing to covert reading at close range.

takeaway: Old 125 kHz proximity cards can be skimmed and cloned from a short distance. Encrypted smart cards with mutual authentication and MFA at sensitive doors are the fix.

scenario: Point-of-sale terminals run one payment application and nothing else. Attackers have been planting new memory-scraping malware variants that signature antivirus misses for days at a time.
stem: Which mitigation is MOST effective for these terminals?

options.text: Application allow listing so only the approved payment software can run
options.why: On a single-purpose device, default-deny execution blocks every new malware variant, whether or not a signature exists yet.

options.text: Updating antivirus signatures every hour instead of every day
options.why: Faster updates still depend on someone writing a signature first, and the variants are evading that for days.

options.text: Full-disk encryption on each terminal's storage
options.why: Memory scrapers read card data from RAM while the system runs, which disk encryption does not protect.

options.text: A stronger local administrator password on each terminal
options.why: The malware is not logging in with the admin password, so stronger credentials do not stop it from running.

takeaway: For fixed-function systems (POS, kiosks, ICS consoles), application allow listing beats signature-based detection against new malware.

stem: An analyst is reviewing a domain controller after a suspected compromise. Which TWO observations MOST strongly suggest the attacker tried to hide their activity? (Select TWO.)

options.text: The Security event log was cleared at 03:12 and now starts with event ID 1102
options.why: Event 1102 records that the audit log was cleared. Clearing logs in the middle of the night is a classic attempt to erase evidence.

options.text: There are no logon events at all between 01:00 and 04:00 on a busy server
options.why: A busy domain controller always logs authentications. A total gap points to logging being stopped or records being deleted.

options.text: Several user accounts were locked out after failed password attempts
options.why: Lockouts indicate guessing attempts. They are noisy, not an attempt to hide.

options.text: CPU use rose sharply during the nightly backup window
options.why: High load during a scheduled backup is expected and not a sign of concealment.

options.text: A user signed in from a new laptop after a hardware refresh
options.why: A new device after a refresh has an obvious legitimate explanation.

takeaway: Missing logs and cleared logs (event ID 1102) are indicators that someone is covering tracks. Ship logs off the host to a SIEM so they survive.

scenario: A cloud provider issues an urgent advisory: a flaw in its virtual network driver lets code running inside one customer's virtual machine execute commands on the physical host and read memory from other customers' virtual machines.
stem: Which vulnerability does the advisory describe?

options.text: VM escape
options.why: Breaking out of a guest to the hypervisor or host, and from there into other guests, is VM escape, the worst-case virtualization flaw.

options.text: Resource reuse
options.why: Resource reuse exposes leftover data when memory or disk is reassigned without being cleared. Here the attacker actively executes code on the host.

options.text: VM sprawl
options.why: VM sprawl is unmanaged growth of virtual machines, an operational problem, not an exploit.

options.text: Privilege escalation inside the guest
options.why: Escalation within one VM stays inside that VM. Reaching the host and other tenants crosses the isolation boundary, which is escape.

takeaway: VM escape crosses from guest to host; resource reuse leaks leftovers between tenants; sprawl is unmanaged growth.

scenario: A caller tells the help desk he is the regional VP, is at an airport about to board, and needs his MFA device reset to a new phone right now. He knows his employee ID and manager's name, both of which appear on social media. The help desk agent feels pressured.
stem: Which control would BEST stop this attack without blocking legitimate urgent resets?

options.text: Verify identity through a separate channel, such as a callback to the number on file
options.why: Verification that the attacker cannot complete with public information, such as a call to the registered number or approval from a known manager, defeats pretexting while still allowing real resets.

options.text: Ask the caller extra personal questions such as their date of birth and office location
options.why: Knowledge-based questions often use information that is public or easy to research, which is exactly what this caller already exploited.

options.text: Refuse all MFA resets requested over the phone
options.why: This stops the attack but also blocks legitimate users who have lost their phones, which the question rules out.

options.text: Train the help desk to recognize urgency as a social engineering tactic
options.why: Training helps, but under pressure people still make mistakes. A required verification step is a stronger control than awareness alone.

takeaway: Pretexting plus urgency and authority beats knowledge-based checks. Out-of-band verification against pre-registered contact details is the reliable control.

scenario: A ransomware group publishes samples of stolen data on its leak site and demands payment both to decrypt files and to keep the data private. The victim has tested, immutable offline backups.
stem: Which additional control would have MOST reduced the leverage the attackers still have?

options.text: Egress monitoring and DLP to detect and block the bulk upload before encryption
options.why: Backups solve the encryption half. The remaining leverage is the stolen data, and only detecting and stopping the exfiltration, for example with egress monitoring and DLP, addresses that.

options.text: A second set of immutable backups stored in another region with a separate account
options.why: More backups make recovery even more certain, but they do nothing about the data the attackers already copied.

options.text: Shorter recovery time objectives for the file servers
options.why: Faster recovery helps availability, not the threat to publish stolen data.

options.text: Full-disk encryption on all file servers
options.why: The data was read and copied while the servers were running and decrypted, so disk encryption would not have stopped the theft.

takeaway: Double extortion has two levers: encryption (answered by backups) and data theft (answered by exfiltration detection, DLP and encrypting sensitive data in use).

scenario: A company's MDM report shows several unrooted Android phones with an app installed from an APK file shared in a group chat. The app requests accessibility permissions and has been reading on-screen text, including one-time codes.
stem: Which vulnerability allowed the app onto the phones, and what MDM control BEST prevents it?

options.text: Side loading, prevented by blocking installs from unknown sources
options.why: Installing an APK from outside the official store is side loading, which skips store vetting. MDM can block unknown sources so only approved stores or managed apps can install.

options.text: Jailbreaking, prevented by detecting and blocking rooted devices
options.why: The phones were not rooted. Side loading works on standard devices when unknown sources are allowed.

options.text: A zero-day flaw in Android, prevented by forcing the latest OS update
options.why: The user installed the app and granted it permissions, so no unknown flaw was exploited.

options.text: Bluesnarfing, prevented by disabling Bluetooth when not in use
options.why: The app arrived as a file in a chat, not over Bluetooth.

takeaway: Side loading installs apps from outside the official store; jailbreaking or rooting removes OS restrictions. They are different, and MDM controls each separately.

scenario: A software distributor still signs downloads using MD5 digests. A researcher shows two different installers, one clean and one with a backdoor, that produce exactly the same MD5 value, so the signature on the clean one also validates the backdoored one.
stem: Which attack has the researcher demonstrated?

options.text: A collision attack against the hash function
options.why: Two different inputs producing the same digest is a collision. Because the signature covers the digest, it validates both files, which is why MD5 and SHA-1 are no longer acceptable for signing.

options.text: A downgrade attack that forced the use of an older algorithm
options.why: Nothing was negotiated or forced. The distributor chose MD5 itself.

options.text: A preimage attack that recovered the installer from its hash
options.why: A preimage attack would find an input matching a given hash. Here the researcher crafted two inputs that share a hash, which is easier and is a collision.

options.text: A key compromise of the distributor's signing certificate
options.why: The private key was never needed. The weakness is in the hash, which lets a valid signature cover a second file.

takeaway: Collisions (two inputs, same hash) defeat signatures built on weak hashes. Use SHA-256 or stronger for signing.

scenario: A hospital is placing an inline IPS between its emergency department network and the systems that hold patient records and imaging. Clinicians must never lose access during a trauma case. The IPS vendor offers fail-open or fail-closed behavior if the appliance crashes.
stem: Which configuration BEST fits the hospital's priorities, and what is the trade-off?

options.text: Fail-open, accepting that traffic passes uninspected while the IPS is down
options.why: When availability is the overriding need, a crashed IPS should pass traffic rather than cut off clinicians. The trade-off is a window with no inspection, which monitoring and fast repair should cover.

options.text: Fail-closed, accepting that clinicians lose access while the IPS is down
options.why: Fail-closed favors security over availability. Losing access during a trauma case is exactly what the requirement forbids.

options.text: Fail-closed, because a medical environment must always put confidentiality first
options.why: Clinical systems usually put availability and integrity first. Confidentiality matters, but not by blocking care when a security appliance fails.

options.text: Fail-open, because an IPS that fails open still blocks known signatures
options.why: A failed-open IPS is effectively a wire. It blocks nothing until it recovers, so this reasoning is wrong even though the setting is right.

takeaway: Fail-open keeps traffic flowing when a security device fails (availability wins); fail-closed blocks it (security wins). Pick based on what the scenario says matters most.

scenario: Employees may use a sanctioned cloud storage service over HTTPS, but the company wants to block uploads to that service while still allowing downloads and viewing. The current firewall filters on IP address, protocol and port only.
stem: Which capability is required?

options.text: A next-generation firewall with TLS inspection and application-level control
options.why: Telling an upload from a download inside HTTPS requires decrypting the traffic and understanding the application's functions, which is what an NGFW with application awareness and TLS inspection does.

options.text: A stateful firewall rule that blocks TCP 443 to the service's IP range
options.why: Uploads and downloads both use TCP 443 to the same addresses, so a layer 4 rule can only block or allow the whole service.

options.text: A network IDS on a span port with a signature for large outbound files
options.why: An IDS on a span port can only alert. It cannot block the upload, and it cannot see inside the encryption without decryption anyway.

options.text: A site-to-site VPN between the office and the cloud storage provider
options.why: A VPN changes how the traffic travels, not what the user is allowed to do in the application.

takeaway: Controlling functions within an application (upload versus download) needs layer 7 inspection, and for HTTPS that means TLS inspection too.

scenario: A company has closed its offices. All 3,000 employees work from home or travel, and nearly every application is SaaS. Backhauling traffic through the headquarters VPN concentrator makes video calls unusable, but security wants consistent web filtering, CASB and zero trust access for everyone.
stem: Which architecture BEST meets these needs?

options.text: Secure access service edge, delivering security from cloud points of presence near users
options.why: SASE puts secure web gateway, CASB, ZTNA and firewalling in the cloud close to each user, so traffic goes straight to SaaS while still getting consistent policy, with no backhaul.

options.text: A larger VPN concentrator at headquarters with a full tunnel for every user
options.why: A bigger concentrator still forces all traffic through headquarters, which is the source of the latency, and there is no longer an office to protect.

options.text: Split tunneling so that all SaaS traffic goes directly to the internet without inspection
options.why: Split tunneling fixes performance by skipping the security stack, which drops the consistent filtering and CASB the requirement asks for.

options.text: SD-WAN connecting each employee's home router to the data center
options.why: SD-WAN optimizes links between sites. It is not a per-user security service, and these users have no branch site.

takeaway: SASE converges networking and security (SWG, CASB, ZTNA, FWaaS) as a cloud service near the user, the fit for a remote-first, SaaS-heavy workforce.

scenario: A developer deploys a web application to a platform-as-a-service offering. A scan finds an outdated, vulnerable version of a third-party library bundled with the application, and an outdated version of the language runtime provided by the platform.
stem: Under the shared responsibility model, who fixes each finding?

options.text: The customer updates the bundled library; the provider updates the runtime
options.why: In PaaS the provider manages the operating system and runtime, while the customer owns its code and the dependencies it ships with that code.

options.text: The provider updates both, because the platform hosts the application
options.why: Hosting the application does not make the provider responsible for what the customer packages inside it.

options.text: The customer updates both, because PaaS customers always manage the runtime
options.why: Managing the runtime is the provider's job in PaaS. In IaaS the customer would manage it.

options.text: The provider updates the library; the customer updates the runtime
options.why: This reverses the model. The customer cannot patch the platform's runtime, and the provider does not maintain customer code.

takeaway: Moving from IaaS to PaaS to SaaS, the provider takes on more of the stack. In PaaS the customer still owns application code, its dependencies, data and access.

scenario: A team manages cloud infrastructure with infrastructure as code. A review finds database passwords and an API key written directly in Terraform files that are committed to a Git repository shared by 60 developers.
stem: Which of the following is the BEST remediation?

options.text: Move the secrets to a secrets manager, rotate them and scan commits for secrets
options.why: The secrets are already exposed in history, so they must be rotated. Storing them in a secrets manager keeps them out of code, and commit scanning stops it from happening again.

options.text: Make the repository private and remove the secrets from the files in a new commit
options.why: The secrets remain in the commit history, and 60 developers still had access. Without rotation, the exposure continues.

options.text: Encode the secrets in Base64 inside the Terraform files
options.why: Base64 is encoding, not encryption. Anyone can reverse it instantly.

options.text: Stop using infrastructure as code and configure the cloud by hand
options.why: This throws away IaC's consistency and auditability without solving secret handling, which is the real problem.

takeaway: Secrets do not belong in code or IaC templates. Once committed, assume they are compromised: rotate, move to a vault and add secret scanning.

scenario: A water utility's SCADA network controls chemical dosing. Its PLCs run vendor firmware that can only be updated during an annual shutdown, and an unplanned reboot can disrupt treatment. A consultant recommends weekly automated patching like the corporate network.
stem: Which of the following is the BEST response to the consultant?

options.text: Keep patching to planned windows and rely on segmentation and monitoring in between
options.why: Industrial systems put availability and safety first, so disruptive patching is scheduled, and compensating controls such as strict segmentation and monitoring cover the gap.

options.text: Adopt weekly automated patching because unpatched systems are always the biggest risk
options.why: Unplanned reboots of dosing controllers could create a safety incident. In ICS, the cure would be worse than the disease.

options.text: Connect the PLCs to the corporate network so they receive patches faster
options.why: Bridging SCADA to the corporate network increases exposure dramatically, which is the opposite of what the environment needs.

options.text: Replace the PLCs with general-purpose servers that can be patched weekly
options.why: General-purpose servers do not provide the deterministic, real-time control PLCs exist for, and replacement is not a realistic security fix.

takeaway: ICS, SCADA and RTOS environments trade patch speed for availability and safety. Segmentation, monitoring and planned maintenance windows compensate.

scenario: Two banks want to run a joint fraud model on combined customer data in a public cloud. Each bank's data is encrypted at rest and in transit, but each bank worries that the cloud provider's administrators could read the data while it is being processed.
stem: Which technology BEST addresses this concern?

options.text: Confidential computing with hardware-based secure enclaves
options.why: The gap is data in use. Secure enclaves keep data encrypted in memory and isolated from the host and its administrators while it is processed.

options.text: Full-disk encryption on the virtual machines with customer-managed keys
options.why: Disk encryption protects data at rest. Once the VM is running, the data in memory is in plaintext.

options.text: TLS 1.3 with mutual authentication between the banks and the cloud
options.why: TLS protects data in transit, which is already covered. It does nothing once the data is being processed.

options.text: Tokenizing customer identifiers before uploading the data
options.why: Tokenization hides identifiers but the model still processes the remaining data in plaintext in memory, and the fraud model may need the real values.

takeaway: Three states, three answers: at rest (disk, database encryption), in transit (TLS, IPsec), in use (secure enclaves, confidential computing).

scenario: A German health insurer moves to a global cloud provider. Regulators require that personal health data never be stored or processed outside the EU. The provider's default backup policy replicates data to the nearest three regions worldwide.
stem: Which control MOST directly addresses the regulatory requirement?

options.text: Restrict storage, processing and backups to EU regions with location policies
options.why: Data sovereignty is about where data lives and is processed. Region restrictions, applied to backups and replicas too, keep every copy inside the required jurisdiction.

options.text: Encrypt the data with keys held by the insurer before uploading it
options.why: Encryption is valuable, but encrypted data replicated outside the EU is still stored outside the EU, which the regulation forbids.

options.text: Sign a data processing agreement with the provider
options.why: An agreement sets obligations but does not by itself stop the default policy from copying data abroad.

options.text: Tokenize member names before storing the data in the cloud
options.why: Health data tied to tokens is still personal data, and the copies would still leave the EU.

takeaway: Sovereignty and geolocation requirements are met by controlling where every copy, including backups and replicas, is stored and processed.

scenario: After an online store added a load balancer in front of four web servers using round-robin, customers report being logged out and losing their carts at random. Each web server keeps session state in its own memory.
stem: Which change would BEST fix the problem while keeping the load balancing?

options.text: Enable session persistence or move session state to a shared store
options.why: Round-robin sends each request to the next server, which does not have the session. Persistence keeps a user on the same server, and a shared session store lets any server handle any request.

options.text: Switch the load balancer from round-robin to least connections
options.why: Least connections still spreads one user's requests across servers, so the session problem remains.

options.text: Add two more web servers to reduce the load on each one
options.why: More servers make it even more likely that a request lands on a server without the session.

options.text: Switch from active-active to active-passive load balancing for the web pool
options.why: Active-passive avoids the problem only by sending everything to one server, which gives up the load balancing the store wanted.

takeaway: Stateful applications behind load balancers need session persistence (sticky sessions) or shared session storage.

scenario: A company replicates its file servers synchronously to a second data center and considers that its backup strategy. Ransomware encrypts the primary file servers at 14:05. The CIO wants to recover to 14:00 at the latest.
stem: What is the MOST likely outcome, and what should have been in place?

options.text: The replica is encrypted too; frequent immutable snapshots or backups were needed
options.why: Synchronous replication faithfully copies the encrypted files within seconds. Recovering to a point before the attack requires point-in-time copies the attacker cannot modify.

options.text: The replica is clean, because replication only copies data on a schedule
options.why: Synchronous replication writes to both sites at once, so the encryption reached the replica almost immediately.

options.text: The replica is clean, because ransomware cannot cross between data centers
options.why: Replication carries any change, malicious or not, so the ransomware does not need to cross anything itself.

options.text: The replica is encrypted, but an RAID 6 array at the primary site will restore the files
options.why: RAID protects against disk failure, not against encrypted data written by the operating system. It mirrors the damage.

takeaway: Replication and RAID copy mistakes and malware instantly. Backups and snapshots, especially immutable or offline ones, give you a point in time to go back to.

scenario: A payment processor wants to prove that its recovery site can actually process transactions correctly. Regulators will not accept a discussion-only exercise, and the business will not accept any interruption to production.
stem: Which type of test BEST fits?

options.text: A parallel processing test that runs real workloads at both sites side by side
options.why: Running the same transactions at the recovery site while production keeps operating proves real processing capability without interrupting customers.

options.text: A full failover test that moves all production workloads over to the recovery site
options.why: A real failover is the most thorough test but risks interrupting production, which the business has ruled out.

options.text: A tabletop exercise that walks the team through the recovery plan
options.why: A tabletop is discussion only, which regulators said they will not accept.

options.text: A simulation in which the team role-plays a data center outage
options.why: A simulation exercises people and decisions, but it does not prove that the systems at the recovery site can actually process transactions.

takeaway: Tabletop: talk it through. Simulation: rehearse the scenario. Parallel processing: run both sites at once with no outage. Failover: actually switch, the most realistic and most disruptive.

scenario: A data center has a diesel generator that takes about 40 seconds to start and stabilize after a utility power failure. During the last outage, every server rebooted before the generator came online.
stem: Which addition MOST directly prevents this?

options.text: A UPS sized to carry the load for at least the generator's start-up time
options.why: A UPS provides immediate battery power, bridging the seconds between the utility failure and the generator taking over.

options.text: A second generator from a different manufacturer
options.why: A second generator also needs time to start, so the gap that caused the reboots remains.

options.text: Dual power supplies in every server
options.why: Dual supplies protect against a failed power supply or circuit. If both are fed from the same failing source, the servers still lose power.

options.text: A managed PDU with remote outlet control
options.why: A PDU distributes and controls power. It does not store energy to cover an outage.

takeaway: Generators handle long outages but start slowly; a UPS bridges the gap and conditions power. You usually need both.

scenario: Remote employees connect through a VPN that sends only traffic for corporate subnets through the tunnel. An incident shows that a laptop was infected while browsing on hotel Wi-Fi, and corporate web filtering never saw the traffic.
stem: Which change would BEST ensure that all of a remote employee's internet traffic is inspected?

options.text: Switch the VPN to a full tunnel so all traffic passes corporate controls
options.why: The current split tunnel lets internet traffic bypass the corporate stack. A full tunnel routes everything through it, so web filtering and other controls see all traffic.

options.text: Increase the VPN encryption from AES-128 to AES-256
options.why: Stronger encryption protects the tunnel, but the problem is traffic that never enters the tunnel.

options.text: Require all employees to disconnect and reconnect the VPN every eight hours
options.why: Reconnecting more often does not change which traffic goes through the tunnel.

options.text: Move the VPN concentrator into the screened subnet
options.why: Where the concentrator sits does not change the split tunneling that lets browsing bypass inspection.

takeaway: Split tunnel: better performance, less visibility. Full tunnel: everything inspected, more load. The question's priority decides which one is correct.

scenario: The security team needs visibility of all traffic between the data center's web tier and database tier, including malformed packets, at a full 10 Gbps. The network team refuses anything that could drop or delay production traffic if it fails.
stem: Which deployment BEST meets both teams' requirements?

options.text: A passive network TAP feeding an IDS sensor
options.why: A hardware TAP copies every packet, including errored frames, at line rate, and it is passive, so if the sensor fails production traffic is unaffected.

options.text: An inline IPS between the web tier and the database tier
options.why: Inline placement can drop or delay traffic if the device fails or is overloaded, which the network team refuses.

options.text: A SPAN port on the core switch feeding an IDS sensor
options.why: SPAN is passive, but switches commonly drop mirrored packets under heavy load and do not forward malformed frames, so it may not give complete visibility at 10 Gbps.

options.text: NetFlow export from the core switch to the SIEM
options.why: NetFlow summarizes connections without packet contents, so the team would not see malformed packets or payloads.

takeaway: Inline means it can block but can also break things; a TAP is passive and complete; SPAN is passive but can drop packets under load.

scenario: A company is enabling 802.1X on every switch port. Laptops authenticate with certificates, but 200 printers and badge readers cannot run an 802.1X supplicant.
stem: Which approach BEST keeps those devices working without leaving their ports wide open?

options.text: Use MAC authentication bypass with profiling and a restricted VLAN
options.why: Devices without supplicants can authenticate by MAC address, profiling reduces spoofing, and a restricted VLAN limits what a spoofed MAC could reach.

options.text: Disable 802.1X on every switch port where a printer or badge reader is connected
options.why: This leaves those ports fully open to anyone who unplugs a printer and connects a laptop.

options.text: Give the printers and badge readers a shared username and password
options.why: Devices that cannot run a supplicant cannot use username and password EAP either, and a shared credential would be weak anyway.

options.text: Move the printers and badge readers to the guest wireless network
options.why: Badge readers and printers need internal resources, and the guest network should only reach the internet.

takeaway: 802.1X needs a supplicant. For headless devices, MAC authentication bypass plus profiling and a restricted VLAN is the usual compensating approach.

scenario: An e-commerce platform was split into 35 microservices that call each other over the internal network. A penetration tester who compromised one container could call the payment service's API directly, because internal calls are trusted by network location alone.
stem: Which control BEST addresses this?

options.text: Mutual TLS between services, with each service authorizing which callers it accepts
options.why: mTLS gives every service a verifiable identity, and per-service authorization means a compromised container can only call what its own identity allows.

options.text: A larger perimeter firewall in front of the container platform
options.why: The attacker was already inside the perimeter. The problem is implicit trust between internal services.

options.text: Running every microservice in the same container to reduce network calls
options.why: Collapsing everything into one container removes isolation entirely and undoes the architecture.

options.text: Encrypting the container images stored in the registry
options.why: Encrypted images protect the images at rest. They do not control which running service may call another.

takeaway: Microservices widen the attack surface. Zero trust between services, using authenticated identities such as mTLS plus per-call authorization, replaces trust by network location.

scenario: A licensing server can only run as a single active instance at a time. The business wants it to survive a hardware failure with no more than a few seconds of interruption.
stem: Which design BEST meets this requirement?

options.text: An active-passive cluster with heartbeat monitoring and automatic failover
options.why: Only one node may be active, so the standby waits and takes over automatically when the heartbeat stops, giving a short interruption.

options.text: An active-active cluster with round-robin load balancing
options.why: Active-active runs several instances at once, which this software does not allow.

options.text: Nightly backups restored to new hardware after a failure
options.why: Restoring from backup takes far longer than a few seconds and loses changes since the last backup.

options.text: A cold site with spare hardware and the installation media
options.why: A cold site takes days to bring up, nowhere near a few seconds.

takeaway: Active-active shares load across live nodes; active-passive keeps a standby ready to take over. Software that allows only one live instance needs active-passive.

scenario: A factory sends production data from its plant network to an analytics service in the cloud over the internet.
stem: Which of the following would protect the confidentiality of the data while it is in transit? (Select TWO.)

options.text: An IPsec site-to-site tunnel using ESP between the plant and the cloud network
options.why: ESP encrypts the packets for the whole trip between the two gateways.

options.text: TLS 1.3 between the plant's data collector and the cloud API
options.why: TLS encrypts the application connection end to end between collector and API.

options.text: SHA-256 hashes calculated for each batch of production data
options.why: Hashes detect changes to the data. They do not hide its contents.

options.text: RAID 10 on the analytics service's storage
options.why: RAID provides availability for stored data. It has nothing to do with data moving over the network.

options.text: An IPsec tunnel using AH only
options.why: AH authenticates packets but does not encrypt them, so the data is still readable in transit.

takeaway: Confidentiality in transit comes from encryption: TLS or IPsec ESP. AH and hashing give integrity, not confidentiality.

scenario: Audit logs show 140 workstations have made RDP and SSH connections to domain controllers and network devices over the past month. Only 12 administrators should ever do this.
stem: Which design change BEST reduces this attack surface while still letting administrators work?

options.text: Allow management protocols only from a hardened, monitored jump server
options.why: Forcing all administration through one hardened, logged chokepoint shrinks the attack surface from 140 machines to one and gives a single place to monitor and record sessions.

options.text: Block RDP and SSH completely at every firewall in the network
options.why: Administrators still need these protocols, so a total block stops legitimate work.

options.text: Move the domain controllers to a different subnet with a new address range
options.why: A new address range does nothing unless access is also restricted, and it is easily discovered.

options.text: Change the default RDP and SSH ports on every server
options.why: Non-standard ports are obscurity. Scanners find them quickly and the access remains open to everyone.

takeaway: Jump servers (bastion hosts) concentrate privileged access into one hardened, monitored path into the management zone.

scenario: A startup runs its back end as serverless functions. A review finds that one function, which only reads from a single storage bucket, runs with an identity that has administrator rights to the entire cloud account.
stem: Which risk does this create, and what is the fix?

options.text: A compromise of that function compromises the whole account; scope its role to read that one bucket
options.why: In serverless the customer still owns identities and permissions. A bug or injected input in the function would inherit administrator rights, so least privilege on the function's role is the fix.

options.text: The provider may patch the function's runtime late; move the function to a virtual machine you patch yourself
options.why: Runtime patching is the provider's job in serverless, and moving to a VM adds operational burden without fixing the excessive permissions.

options.text: The function could run out of memory; increase its memory allocation
options.why: Memory limits affect performance and cost, not the security exposure of an over-privileged identity.

options.text: The function's code is stored in plaintext; encrypt the deployment package
options.why: Encrypting the package protects code at rest but leaves the administrator role untouched.

takeaway: Serverless removes server patching from your list but not identity and permissions. Over-privileged function roles are one of the biggest serverless risks.

scenario: A tax preparation firm's systems slow to a crawl every April, the help desk is overwhelmed, and last year the SOC missed alerts because analysts were helping with tickets.
stem: Which activity BEST addresses this recurring problem?

options.text: Capacity planning that covers people, technology and infrastructure for the seasonal peak
options.why: The problem spans staffing, system resources and infrastructure at a predictable peak. Capacity planning addresses all three before the peak arrives.

options.text: A disaster recovery test of the firm's warm site
options.why: Nothing has failed. The systems and people are overloaded by predictable demand, which a DR test does not address.

options.text: A tabletop exercise on responding to a DDoS attack
options.why: The slowdown comes from legitimate seasonal demand, not an attack.

options.text: Doubling the SIEM's log retention period
options.why: Longer retention does not help analysts who are too busy to look at alerts in the first place.

takeaway: Capacity planning considers people, technology and infrastructure. Predictable peaks are a planning problem, not an incident.

scenario: A retailer with 400 stores lets each store manager configure their own store's firewall. Audits find 400 different rule sets, many with any-any rules added to fix connectivity problems quickly.
stem: Which change BEST addresses the root cause?

options.text: Centrally manage store firewalls with a standard template that local staff cannot override
options.why: Decentralized administration produced inconsistent, weak configurations. Central management with an enforced baseline makes every store consistent and auditable.

options.text: Train every store manager on firewall rule writing
options.why: Training helps, but 400 independent administrators will still drift apart. The issue is the decentralized model itself.

options.text: Replace the store firewalls with higher-throughput models
options.why: Throughput is not the problem. The weak rules would simply be copied onto faster hardware.

options.text: Ask each store manager to submit their rule set once a year for review
options.why: Annual reviews catch problems long after they are introduced and do not stop managers adding any-any rules in between.

takeaway: Decentralized administration trades consistency for local flexibility. When consistency fails, centralize management and enforce a baseline.

scenario: A scan returns two findings. Finding 1: CVSS 9.8 remote code execution on a lab server on an isolated network with no route to production. Finding 2: CVSS 7.5 authentication bypass on the internet-facing VPN appliance; the CVE appears on CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities list. The team can only patch one system this week.
stem: Which should be remediated FIRST, and why?

options.text: The VPN appliance, because it is exposed and actively exploited
options.why: Prioritization weighs exploitability and exposure, not just the base score. An internet-facing system with a flaw already being exploited in the wild carries far more real risk than an isolated lab box.

options.text: The lab server, because CVSS 9.8 is critical and must always be fixed before a 7.5
options.why: The base score ignores environment. An isolated lab server with no route to production is hard to reach, so its real-world risk is lower.

options.text: Neither, until a credentialed scan confirms that both findings are real
options.why: Confirmation matters, but a known exploited flaw on an exposed VPN should not wait for a second scan. You can validate and patch in the same window.

options.text: The lab server, because remote code execution is always worse than an authentication bypass on any network
options.why: Bypassing authentication on a VPN can give an attacker the whole network. The type of flaw matters less than how reachable and how exploited it is.

takeaway: CVSS base scores rank severity in a vacuum. Real prioritization adds exposure, active exploitation (such as KEV) and the asset's importance.

scenario: A non-credentialed scan flags 30 Red Hat servers as vulnerable to an OpenSSH CVE because the banner shows an old version number. The operations team says Red Hat backports security fixes without changing the upstream version string.
stem: What should the analyst do NEXT?

options.text: Validate with a credentialed scan or the vendor's package advisory
options.why: Version banners often hide backported fixes. A credentialed scan or the vendor's errata shows whether the fixed package is actually installed, which confirms or dismisses the finding.

options.text: Mark all 30 findings as false positives because the operations team vouched for them
options.why: Accepting an explanation without evidence risks dismissing a real vulnerability. Findings should be verified, not waived on someone's word.

options.text: Upgrade OpenSSH from source on all 30 servers to remove the old version string from the banner
options.why: Replacing vendor packages with source builds breaks supportability and future patching, and may not even be necessary.

options.text: Change the SSH banner so the scanner stops reporting the version
options.why: Hiding the banner only suppresses the symptom. It does not tell you whether the servers are actually vulnerable.

takeaway: Confirm before you remediate or dismiss. Banner-based findings on distributions that backport fixes are a common source of false positives.

scenario: A quarterly scan of 800 Windows servers reports almost nothing beyond open ports, yet the patch team knows dozens of servers are missing months of updates.
stem: Which change would MOST improve the accuracy of the results?

options.text: Run credentialed scans with a least-privilege scanning account
options.why: A credentialed scan logs in and checks installed patches, versions and configuration, producing far fewer false negatives than looking at the server from outside.

options.text: Increase the scan frequency from quarterly to weekly using the same settings
options.why: Scanning more often with the same blind spot just repeats the same false negatives more often.

options.text: Switch to an intrusive scan that attempts to exploit each open port
options.why: Exploit attempts can crash servers and still would not reveal missing patches for services that are not exposed.

options.text: Scan from the internet so that the results reflect what an attacker sees
options.why: An external view sees even less of the patch state than the current internal, non-credentialed scan.

takeaway: Non-credentialed scans show the attacker's outside view and miss a lot; credentialed scans see installed software and missing patches.

scenario: A critical patch for a payroll application server will break the vendor's software, and the vendor's fix is 90 days away. The business cannot run payroll without the application.
stem: Which response is MOST appropriate?

options.text: A documented, time-limited exception with compensating controls, approved by the risk owner
options.why: When remediation is not possible, a formal exception records the risk, sets an expiry date, names who accepted it and adds compensating controls such as isolation and monitoring until the fix arrives.

options.text: Install the patch anyway because critical vulnerabilities must always be patched within 14 days
options.why: Breaking payroll causes certain business harm. Policy deadlines usually allow approved exceptions for exactly this situation.

options.text: Remove the server from the vulnerability scanner's scope until the vendor releases the fix
options.why: Hiding the finding removes visibility without reducing risk, and the system could be forgotten after 90 days.

options.text: Transfer the risk by asking the vendor to sign an indemnity letter
options.why: An indemnity letter may shift some financial impact, but it leaves the server exposed and does nothing to stop an attack.

takeaway: Can't patch yet? Document an exception or exemption with an owner, an expiry and compensating controls. Never just hide the finding.

scenario: The server team reports that the 42 critical findings from last month's scan have been remediated, and the ticket is ready to close.
stem: What is the BEST way to validate the remediation?

options.text: Rescan the affected systems and confirm the findings no longer appear
options.why: Validation means independent evidence. Rescanning shows whether each fix actually took effect, catching missed servers or failed installs.

options.text: Ask the server team to sign off that every patch was installed
options.why: Self-attestation is not verification. Patches fail silently, and servers get missed.

options.text: Close the ticket and check again during next quarter's scheduled scan
options.why: Waiting a quarter leaves any failed remediation exposed for months without anyone knowing.

options.text: Review the change tickets to confirm that changes were approved
options.why: Approved changes show intent, not outcome. They do not prove the vulnerabilities are gone.

takeaway: Vulnerability management ends with validation: rescan, audit or otherwise verify, then report.

scenario: A company is retiring 300 laptops with self-encrypting SSDs that held customer data. The laptops will be sold to a refurbisher, so the drives must remain usable, and auditors require proof of sanitization.
stem: Which approach BEST meets these requirements?

options.text: Cryptographic erase of each SSD, with a certificate of sanitization per drive
options.why: Crypto erase destroys the drive's encryption key, instantly making the data unrecoverable while leaving the drive reusable, and the certificates satisfy the auditors.

options.text: Degauss each SSD and record the serial numbers before the laptops are shipped out
options.why: Degaussing works on magnetic media only. It does not erase flash memory and it provides false assurance.

options.text: Shred each SSD and obtain a certificate of destruction from a vendor
options.why: Shredding is thorough and well documented, but it destroys the drives, which conflicts with selling the laptops.

options.text: Format each SSD with a quick format and reinstall the operating system
options.why: A quick format leaves most data recoverable, especially on SSDs where wear leveling keeps old blocks around.

takeaway: Reuse means sanitize (crypto erase or secure erase for SSDs); no reuse means destroy. Degaussing only works on magnetic media. Keep certificates either way.

scenario: A law firm wants to buy phones for its attorneys, keep full management control including remote wipe, and still let attorneys use the phones for personal email and photos.
stem: Which mobile deployment model fits BEST?

options.text: COPE
options.why: Corporate-owned, personally enabled: the firm buys and fully manages the phone, while allowing reasonable personal use.

options.text: BYOD, with an MDM agent installed on the personal devices that the attorneys already own
options.why: BYOD means the attorneys own the phones, but the firm wants to buy them, and full control of a personal device is hard to justify.

options.text: CYOD, where attorneys pick a model from an approved list for business use only
options.why: Choose your own device lets users pick from a list, but the scenario's key point is allowing personal use on a company-owned, fully managed phone.

options.text: VDI, with attorneys reaching a hosted mobile desktop from any device they happen to have
options.why: VDI is a way to deliver desktops, not a device ownership model, and it does not provide a managed phone.

takeaway: BYOD: user owns it. COPE: company owns it, personal use allowed. CYOD: user chooses from an approved list. Ownership and personal use are the deciding facts.

scenario: A company is evaluating a commercial file-parsing library delivered only as a compiled binary. The vendor will not provide source code. Security wants to find crashes and memory corruption bugs before deployment.
stem: Which testing approach is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Dynamic analysis by fuzzing the library with malformed files
options.why: Without source code, the practical way to find parsing bugs is to run the library and feed it huge numbers of malformed inputs, watching for crashes and memory errors.

options.text: Static code analysis of the library's source code before it is integrated into the product
options.why: Static analysis needs source code, which the vendor will not provide.

options.text: A manual peer code review of the integration code written by the in-house developers
options.why: Reviewing in-house code is useful, but the bugs in question would be inside the vendor's library, which the review cannot see.

options.text: Verifying the library's code signing certificate
options.why: A valid signature proves who published the library and that it was not altered. It says nothing about bugs inside it.

takeaway: Static analysis reads code without running it; dynamic analysis and fuzzing run it with crafted inputs, which is the only option for a black-box binary.

scenario: A university's mailing list forwards messages from external senders to 5,000 subscribers. After the receiving mail servers start enforcing DMARC, forwarded messages from domains with strict policies are rejected. Investigation shows SPF fails on the forwarded copies.
stem: Why does SPF fail, and which mechanism can still pass DMARC for these messages?

options.text: The forwarder's IP is not in the sender's SPF record; an intact DKIM signature still passes
options.why: SPF checks the connecting server's IP, which is now the university's, not the original sender's. DKIM signs the message itself, so if the list does not alter the signed parts, the signature still verifies and satisfies DMARC.

options.text: Forwarding strips the sender's DMARC record; republishing it with a longer TTL fixes it
options.why: DMARC records are looked up in DNS by receivers. Forwarding does not strip them, and TTL has nothing to do with this failure.

options.text: SPF only works over TLS; enabling STARTTLS on the list server makes SPF pass again
options.why: SPF is unrelated to transport encryption. It fails because the sending IP changed.

options.text: The subscribers' own SPF records block forwarding; asking them to add the list server fixes it
options.why: SPF is evaluated against the sender's domain, not the recipients'. Recipients' records play no part.

takeaway: SPF validates the sending IP and breaks on forwarding; DKIM validates a signature on the message and survives forwarding if the content is not modified. DMARC passes if either aligns.

scenario: Attackers keep spoofing a company's domain in phishing emails. The company uses a CRM platform, a marketing service and a ticketing system that all send mail as its domain, and nobody is sure which other services do. Its DMARC record does not exist yet.
stem: Which approach BEST stops the spoofing without breaking legitimate mail?

options.text: Publish DMARC at p=none, align every legitimate sender from the reports, then enforce
options.why: Monitoring mode reveals every service sending as the domain. Once all of them are aligned with SPF or DKIM, enforcing quarantine and then reject blocks spoofing without collateral damage.

options.text: Publish DMARC at p=reject immediately so that all spoofed mail is blocked starting today
options.why: Rejecting before inventorying senders would bounce legitimate CRM, marketing and ticketing mail, and possibly others nobody knew about.

options.text: Add every known sender to the SPF record and skip DMARC entirely
options.why: SPF alone tells receivers nothing about what to do with failures and does not check the visible From address, so spoofing continues.

options.text: Block the company's own domain at the inbound email gateway
options.why: This might stop some spoofed internal mail, but it does nothing for customers and partners receiving spoofed messages, and it breaks real internal mail.

takeaway: Roll DMARC out in stages: p=none to discover senders, align them with SPF or DKIM, then quarantine, then reject.

scenario: Sales staff spend most of their time on hotel and customer Wi-Fi without a VPN. The company wants to block access to known malicious and newly registered domains on those laptops wherever they are, with as little performance impact as possible.
stem: Which solution BEST fits?

options.text: An agent-based DNS filtering service that applies policy on any network
options.why: A lightweight agent sends lookups to a filtering resolver from any network, blocking bad domains before a connection is made, with almost no performance cost.

options.text: A proxy server in the headquarters data center with a PAC file on each laptop
options.why: A central proxy only filters traffic routed back to headquarters, adding latency for staff who rarely use the VPN.

options.text: A next-generation firewall at the headquarters internet edge
options.why: Laptops on hotel Wi-Fi never pass through the headquarters firewall.

options.text: Host file entries for known malicious domains pushed by group policy
options.why: Static hosts entries cannot keep up with constantly changing malicious and newly registered domains.

takeaway: Roaming users need protection that travels with the device: agent-based DNS filtering or a cloud SWG, not a central appliance they never pass through.

scenario: A web server was compromised through a vulnerable plugin, and the attacker read files outside the web root. The audit log shows SELinux recorded "avc: denied" messages for every one of those reads, yet the reads succeeded.
stem: What is the MOST likely explanation?

options.text: SELinux was in permissive mode, which logs violations without blocking them
options.why: Denial messages for actions that still succeeded are the signature of permissive mode. Enforcing mode would have blocked the reads and logged the same messages.

options.text: SELinux was disabled, so the kernel ignored its policy entirely
options.why: A disabled SELinux would not log any avc messages at all.

options.text: The attacker had root, and SELinux cannot restrict the root user
options.why: SELinux mandatory access control does restrict root processes, which is one of its main purposes.

options.text: The policy allowed the reads, and the logged denials were only false positives
options.why: If the policy allowed them, SELinux would not log denials. The log shows the policy forbade the reads.

takeaway: SELinux permissive mode logs what it would block but enforces nothing. Production systems need enforcing mode.

scenario: Engineers occasionally copy design files labeled Confidential to USB drives to work at home. Network DLP on the email gateway and web proxy is already in place, but it never sees these copies.
stem: Which control BEST closes this gap?

options.text: Endpoint DLP that blocks copying labeled files to removable media
options.why: Copying to USB never touches the network, so only an agent on the endpoint can see the file's label and block or log the copy.

options.text: A firewall rule that blocks outbound connections from the engineering VLAN to the internet
options.why: Copying to a USB drive does not use the network at all, so firewall rules cannot see it.

options.text: Full-disk encryption on the engineers' laptops
options.why: FDE protects the laptop if it is stolen. It does nothing to stop a logged-in user copying files to a USB drive.

options.text: A CASB that monitors sanctioned and unsanctioned cloud application use by the engineering team
options.why: A CASB governs cloud application use. It does not see local copies to removable media.

takeaway: Network DLP sees what crosses the network; endpoint DLP sees local actions such as USB copies, printing and clipboard use.

scenario: An audit finds employees who changed departments years ago still hold access from their old roles. The company already removes access when people leave.
stem: Which process would BEST catch this privilege creep going forward?

options.text: Periodic access reviews in which managers attest to each user's current access
options.why: Regular recertification asks managers to confirm or revoke each person's access, catching rights left over from earlier roles.

options.text: Stronger password requirements for accounts that have access to sensitive systems
options.why: Password strength does nothing about whether the person should hold the access at all.

options.text: Disabling accounts after 90 days of inactivity
options.why: These users are active, so inactivity rules never trigger. The problem is excess access, not unused accounts.

options.text: Identity proofing when each employee is first hired
options.why: Proofing confirms who someone is at onboarding. It does not track how their access accumulates later.

takeaway: Deprovisioning handles leavers; access reviews and attestation handle movers whose old permissions linger (privilege creep).

scenario: A hospital wants clinicians to open a patient chart only if they are assigned to that patient's care team, are on shift, are on a hospital-managed device and are on the hospital network. Assignments change hourly.
stem: Which access control model BEST supports these rules?

options.text: Attribute-based access control
options.why: ABAC evaluates many attributes together (user, resource, device and environment), which is what care-team membership, shift, device and location require, and it adapts as attributes change.

options.text: Role-based access control with a separate role for each care team that clinicians join and leave
options.why: Roles would explode in number with hourly team changes, and RBAC alone does not consider device or location.

options.text: Mandatory access control with classification labels on charts
options.why: MAC matches clearances to labels. It does not handle shifts, care-team assignments or device posture.

options.text: Discretionary access control in which each patient's physician grants access to colleagues
options.why: Leaving access to individual owners is inconsistent and does not enforce the device, shift and network conditions.

takeaway: When access depends on several changing conditions at once (who, what, when, where, which device), the answer is ABAC.

scenario: Twelve engineers hold permanent Domain Admin membership but use it only a few times a month. An attacker who phished one engineer immediately had full domain control.
stem: Which change MOST reduces this exposure while still letting engineers do admin work?

options.text: Just-in-time elevation that grants Domain Admin for an approved, time-limited task
options.why: With no standing privileged membership, a phished account normally holds no admin rights. Elevation happens only on request, for a limited time, and is logged.

options.text: Requiring the engineers to use 20-character passwords and change them every 60 days
options.why: Phishing captures whatever the password is, so length and rotation would not have prevented the attack.

options.text: Moving the twelve engineers into a single shared administrator account that is vaulted
options.why: Sharing one account removes accountability and still leaves a standing admin credential to steal.

options.text: Monitoring Domain Admin logons with a SIEM alert
options.why: Alerts help detect misuse but do not reduce the standing privilege the attacker used.

takeaway: Standing privilege is the risk. Just-in-time access, password vaulting and ephemeral credentials shrink it.

scenario: The same web server has been reinfected with a web shell three times in two months. Each time, the team removed the shell, restored the site and closed the incident.
stem: Which step did the team MOST likely skip?

options.text: Root cause analysis to find and fix how the attacker keeps getting in
options.why: Removing the web shell treats the symptom. Without finding the entry point, such as a vulnerable plugin or stolen credentials, the attacker simply returns.

options.text: Notifying law enforcement about the repeated compromise
options.why: Notification may be appropriate, but it would not stop the reinfections.

options.text: Restoring the server from a backup taken before the first infection
options.why: A clean restore does not close the hole the attacker used, so reinfection would follow.

options.text: Increasing the retention of the web server access logs
options.why: Better logs help investigation, but only if someone actually performs the investigation.

takeaway: Recurring incidents mean the root cause was never found. Eradication is incomplete until the entry point is fixed.

scenario: Legal counsel tells the CISO that a former employee is likely to sue the company. The email system automatically deletes messages older than 180 days.
stem: What should the CISO do FIRST?

options.text: Place a legal hold that suspends deletion for the relevant mailboxes and records
options.why: Once litigation is reasonably anticipated, relevant data must be preserved. A legal hold overrides the normal retention schedule so evidence is not destroyed.

options.text: Export every mailbox in the company to offline storage
options.why: Overcollecting is costly and unnecessary. A hold should cover the relevant custodians and data.

options.text: Let the 180-day deletion policy continue because it was in place before the dispute
options.why: Allowing deletion after litigation is anticipated can be treated as spoliation of evidence, even if the policy is routine.

options.text: Start e-discovery and send the relevant messages to opposing counsel
options.why: Production through e-discovery comes later, through counsel. The first step is preservation.

takeaway: Anticipated litigation triggers a legal hold first: preserve, then collect and produce through e-discovery.

scenario: An investigator removes the hard drive from a suspect's powered-off workstation. The case may go to court, so the defense will challenge whether the evidence was altered.
stem: Which procedure BEST preserves the drive's integrity as evidence?

options.text: Image it through a write blocker, hash both drive and image, and log the custody
options.why: A write blocker prevents any change to the original, matching hashes prove the image is identical, and the custody record shows who handled it and when.

options.text: Boot the workstation once more to confirm that the drive still works before imaging it
options.why: Booting writes to the drive (logs, timestamps, swap), altering the evidence before it is preserved.

options.text: Copy the user's files to an external drive with the operating system's copy function
options.why: A file copy misses deleted data and slack space and changes access metadata. It is not a forensic image.

options.text: Encrypt the original drive so that nobody else can tamper with it
options.why: Encrypting the original modifies it, which destroys its value as unaltered evidence.

takeaway: Forensic acquisition: write blocker, bit-for-bit image, hashes of original and copy, and an unbroken chain of custody.

scenario: A phishing email delivered a ZIP file to 40 users. The analyst must determine which users actually opened the archive and ran the program inside, and what it launched.
stem: Which data source would BEST answer this?

options.text: Endpoint logs from EDR, showing process creation and the parent processes
options.why: Only the endpoint sees a program execute and what it spawns. EDR process telemetry shows who ran the file and the process tree that followed.

options.text: Email gateway logs, showing which recipients received the message and the attachment
options.why: Gateway logs show delivery, not whether anyone opened the archive or ran the program.

options.text: Firewall logs, showing outbound connections from each workstation during the day
options.why: Firewall logs might show suspicious traffic later, but they cannot show which program ran on which host.

options.text: NetFlow from the core switch
options.why: NetFlow records conversations between addresses. It has no visibility into processes on endpoints.

takeaway: Pick the data source that observes the event directly: execution is seen on the endpoint, delivery at the gateway, and connections at the firewall.

scenario: An analyst knows a workstation transferred about 2 GB to an external address last night over an unencrypted protocol. Legal now needs to know exactly which files were sent.
stem: Which data source can answer this question?

options.text: A full packet capture of the traffic
options.why: Packet captures contain the payloads, so the transferred files can be reconstructed from an unencrypted session. Metadata sources cannot do this.

options.text: NetFlow records for the workstation
options.why: NetFlow shows who talked to whom, when and how many bytes. It contains no file names or content.

options.text: The firewall's connection log
options.why: Connection logs record addresses, ports, actions and byte counts, not the content.

options.text: DNS query logs
options.why: DNS logs show which names were looked up. They cannot show what data was sent afterward.

takeaway: Metadata (NetFlow, firewall and DNS logs) shows that something happened; only packet captures show what was in it.

scenario: An audit of network management finds FTP used to move configuration backups, SNMPv2c with the community string "public" for monitoring, and Telnet used to administer switches.
stem: Which replacements BEST address the findings? (Select THREE.)

options.text: SFTP for the configuration backups
options.why: SFTP runs over SSH, encrypting both credentials and file contents, unlike FTP which sends both in clear text.

options.text: SNMPv3 with authentication and privacy enabled
options.why: SNMPv3 adds per-user authentication and encryption, replacing clear-text community strings.

options.text: SSH for switch administration
options.why: SSH encrypts the management session, replacing Telnet's clear-text logins.

options.text: TFTP for the configuration backups
options.why: TFTP has no authentication or encryption at all, so it is worse than FTP.

options.text: SNMPv2c with a longer, random community string
options.why: A longer community string is still sent in clear text and offers no real authentication.

options.text: HTTP-based web management on the switches
options.why: Plain HTTP sends credentials in clear text, the same weakness as Telnet.

takeaway: Know the secure replacements: FTP to SFTP or FTPS, Telnet to SSH, SNMPv1/v2c to SNMPv3, HTTP to HTTPS, LDAP to LDAPS.

scenario: A security analyst must collect evidence from a running Windows server suspected of hosting a memory-resident backdoor. The server will be rebuilt afterward.
stem: Which actions are appropriate? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Capture a memory image before shutting the server down
options.why: A memory-resident backdoor lives in RAM, which is lost at power-off, so memory comes first in the order of volatility.

options.text: Record a hash of each image and keep a chain of custody log
options.why: Hashes prove the evidence has not changed, and the custody log documents everyone who handled it.

options.text: Run a full antivirus scan on the server before collecting anything
options.why: Scanning changes files and timestamps and may remove artifacts before they are preserved.

options.text: Reboot into safe mode so that the backdoor cannot run during collection
options.why: Rebooting destroys the volatile memory that holds the backdoor.

options.text: Copy suspicious files to the analyst's laptop using drag and drop
options.why: Ad hoc copies alter metadata and are not forensically sound images.

takeaway: Volatile first, hash everything, document custody, and do not let tools or reboots change the evidence before it is preserved.

scenario: Users on the warehouse floor keep dropping off Wi-Fi near the loading docks. A tool shows a strong unknown signal on the same channel, and coverage maps are years out of date.
stem: What should the wireless team do FIRST?

options.text: Perform a site survey and produce a heat map of coverage and interference
options.why: A site survey measures actual signal strength, dead zones and interference sources, giving the evidence needed to move access points, change channels or find the unknown transmitter.

options.text: Double the transmit power on every access point across the whole warehouse floor
options.why: Raising power without data often increases co-channel interference and can extend the network into the parking lot.

options.text: Switch the SSID from WPA2 to WPA3 to stop the disconnections
options.why: The symptoms are coverage and interference, which the security mode does not affect.

options.text: Hide the SSID so that the unknown device cannot see the network
options.why: Hiding the SSID does not stop interference and offers almost no security benefit.

takeaway: Wireless problems start with measurement: a site survey and heat map show coverage, dead zones, overlap and rogue or interfering signals.

scenario: Tier 1 analysts spend most of their shift on the same steps for every reported phishing email: extract URLs and attachments, check reputation services, search for other recipients and delete copies. Response times are falling behind.
stem: Which solution BEST reduces the workload while keeping responses consistent?

options.text: A SOAR playbook that automates the enrichment, search and removal steps
options.why: Repetitive, well-defined steps are what orchestration and automation are for. A playbook runs them the same way every time and frees analysts for judgment calls.

options.text: A larger SIEM storage allocation so that more email logs can be searched
options.why: More storage does not perform any of the manual steps the analysts are drowning in.

options.text: An additional email gateway from a second vendor in front of the current one
options.why: A second gateway might catch more phishing, but it does nothing about handling the reports that still arrive.

options.text: A policy requiring users to delete suspicious emails without reporting them
options.why: Ignoring reports loses the early warning they provide and leaves the same message in other inboxes.

takeaway: SIEM collects and correlates; SOAR orchestrates and automates the response. Repetitive playbook steps are the SOAR use case.

scenario: A SIEM rule alerts whenever any account fails to log in five times in ten minutes. It fires 1,800 times a day, almost all from a service account with an expired password and from users mistyping passwords on Monday mornings. Analysts now ignore it.
stem: Which action BEST improves this rule's value?

options.text: Fix the service account and tune the rule's thresholds and context
options.why: Alert tuning removes known benign sources and adds context (many accounts from one source, failures followed by success) so the rule fires on attacks rather than noise.

options.text: Disable the rule because failed logins are already blocked by account lockout
options.why: Disabling it removes visibility into password spraying and brute force, which lockout does not always stop.

options.text: Raise the alert's severity so that analysts cannot ignore it
options.why: Making a noisy alert louder makes alert fatigue worse, not better.

options.text: Forward every alert from the rule to the CISO's inbox for review
options.why: Moving the noise to someone else does not make it useful.

takeaway: Alert fatigue is fixed by tuning (thresholds, exclusions, context), not by turning rules off or turning them up.

scenario: Twice this year, an attacker changed the web server's configuration to inject a credit card skimmer script, and nobody noticed for weeks. The server's files rarely change outside approved releases.
stem: Which control would detect this kind of change MOST quickly?

options.text: File integrity monitoring on the web root and configuration files
options.why: FIM baselines file hashes and alerts on unexpected changes, which is exactly what injecting a script into rarely changing files produces.

options.text: A weekly vulnerability scan of the web server from an internal scanner
options.why: A vulnerability scan looks for known weaknesses, not for unexpected changes to files.

options.text: A web application firewall blocking SQL injection attempts on the site
options.why: A WAF may block some attacks, but it would not notice a configuration file already being modified.

options.text: NetFlow monitoring of the web server's outbound traffic
options.why: Skimmers often send card data from the customer's browser, not from the server, so NetFlow may show nothing unusual.

takeaway: FIM detects unauthorized changes to files that should be stable, such as web content, configs and system binaries.

scenario: A threat intelligence report describes a group that persists by creating scheduled tasks named like legitimate updaters and moves laterally with remote WMI. No alerts have fired in the company's environment.
stem: Which activity BEST uses this intelligence?

options.text: A hypothesis-driven threat hunt for such scheduled tasks and WMI use
options.why: Threat hunting assumes a breach may already have happened and proactively searches for the described behavior, which catches activity that slipped past existing detections.

options.text: Waiting for the SIEM to raise an alert before investigating
options.why: That is reactive by definition, and the report suggests the group may evade existing alerts.

options.text: Running a penetration test against the external perimeter
options.why: A pen test checks whether someone could get in. It does not look for an adversary who may already be inside.

options.text: Blocking all scheduled tasks on every endpoint
options.why: Scheduled tasks are used by legitimate software, so a blanket block would break systems and is not an investigation.

takeaway: Threat hunting is proactive and hypothesis-driven, often seeded by threat intelligence, and looks for what alerts missed.

scenario: A company wants to make sure that 6,000 Windows laptops all enforce the same screen lock timeout, disable legacy SMBv1, and block running executables from user download folders, and that local users cannot change these settings.
stem: Which tool is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Group Policy applied from Active Directory
options.why: Group Policy centrally enforces operating system settings on domain-joined Windows machines and reapplies them if users try to change them.

options.text: A SIEM correlation rule that alerts when settings differ
options.why: A SIEM can detect differences, but it does not apply or enforce the settings.

options.text: A vulnerability scanner with a Windows hardening policy
options.why: A scanner reports configuration gaps. It does not push settings to 6,000 laptops.

options.text: A one-time configuration script run by the help desk during deployment
options.why: A one-off script cannot stop users or software from changing settings afterward.

takeaway: Configuration enforcement at scale uses central policy tools (Group Policy, MDM or UEM), not detection tools or one-time scripts.

scenario: A company automated user provisioning with dozens of scripts written by one engineer, who has now left. A change in the HR system's API silently broke account deprovisioning, and nobody understands the scripts well enough to fix them quickly.
stem: Which automation drawback does this BEST illustrate?

options.text: Technical debt and complexity that create a single point of failure
options.why: Undocumented, person-dependent scripts are technical debt, and when they break, a critical process (deprovisioning) fails with nobody able to support it.

options.text: Reduced reaction time, because automation is slower than manual work
options.why: Automation usually improves reaction time. The problem here is supportability, not speed.

options.text: Inability to enforce baselines, because scripts cannot apply standards
options.why: Enforcing baselines is a benefit of automation. The failure here is maintainability.

options.text: Lower employee retention, because automation makes jobs less interesting
options.why: Automation is usually cited as improving retention by removing tedious work, and the scenario is about a broken integration.

takeaway: Automation drawbacks to know: complexity, cost, single point of failure, technical debt and ongoing supportability.

scenario: A federal contractor must prove that 900 Linux servers comply with a published hardening benchmark and produce machine-readable results for auditors every month.
stem: Which approach BEST meets this requirement?

options.text: Automated SCAP scans against the benchmark's checklist
options.why: SCAP-compatible tools evaluate systems against standardized benchmark content (such as CIS or DISA STIG) and produce machine-readable compliance reports at scale.

options.text: Manual review of a random sample of 20 servers each month
options.why: Sampling does not prove that all 900 comply, and manual results are not machine-readable.

options.text: A penetration test of the Linux servers once a year
options.why: A pen test looks for exploitable weaknesses, not line-by-line compliance with a benchmark, and once a year misses the monthly requirement.

options.text: NetFlow analysis of traffic to and from the Linux servers
options.why: Traffic patterns say nothing about whether the servers' configurations match the benchmark.

takeaway: SCAP plus benchmarks (CIS, STIG) gives automated, standardized, machine-readable configuration compliance checks.

scenario: Contractors plug their own laptops into conference room ports. The company wants unmanaged or unpatched devices to reach only a remediation portal and the internet, while compliant corporate laptops get full access.
